articles.title: Starlink tem uma 'irmã militar' controlada pelos EUA; entenda o que é a Starshield | G1
articles.standfirst: Empresa atende governos e forças armadas com comunicações protegidas e satélites de reconhecimento. Diferenças entre os serviços ganharam destaque após queixas da Ucrânia sobre restrições de acesso.
articles.summary: Empresa atende governos e forças armadas com comunicações protegidas e satélites de reconhecimento. Diferenças entre os serviços ganharam destaque após queixas da Ucrânia.
articles.body:
Em imagem de arquivo, soldado ucrnaiano prepara sistema de internet por satélite da Starlink em sua posição na frente de batalha na cidade de Avdiivka, na Ucrânia, em fevereiro de 2024. — Foto: Inna Varenytsia/ Reuters

A queixa da Ucrânia de que a SpaceX, de Elon Musk, teria restringido os serviços Starlink de "nível militar" voltou a chamar a atenção para as diferenças entre o Starlink, serviço comercial de internet via satélite da empresa, e o Starshield, versão militar desenvolvida para o Pentágono.

"Os sistemas Starshield são propriedade e estão sob controle do governo dos Estados Unidos", escreveu Musk nesta quarta-feira (14/10) numa postagem no X, acrescentando que quaisquer limites de velocidade ou de uso são decididos pelos militares ou pelo presidente dos EUA.

Já "o Starlink é um serviço comercial pertencente e controlado pela SpaceX. Seu uso está limitado a atividades civis ou defensivas e não pode ser empregado em ações militares ofensivas, pois isso seria inadequado para uma empresa comercial".

Starlink e Starshield não são sistemas completamente separados, mas também não são a mesma coisa:

O Starlink é o serviço civil de internet administrado pela própria SpaceX.

O Starshield é a versão governamental e conta com alguns satélites próprios para reconhecimento e comunicação militar, além de oferecer criptografia mais robusta.

Ambos, porém, operam com a mesma tecnologia e, em parte, utilizam os mesmos satélites.

Principal fonte de lucro da SpaceX, o Starlink é um serviço que utiliza satélites em órbita baixa da Terra para fornecer acesso à internet, principalmente em áreas remotas.

Trata-se de uma rede composta por mais de 11 mil satélites que fornecem internet de alta velocidade diretamente aos equipamentos dos usuários. Seus cerca de 13 milhões de assinantes incluem moradores, excursionistas, empresas de navegação e grandes companhias aéreas.

Desde o lançamento dos primeiros satélites Starlink, em 2019, a bordo dos foguetes reutilizáveis da SpaceX, a empresa formou uma vasta rede em órbita baixa que cobre grande parte do planeta.

O sistema oferece conexões mais rápidas do que as fornecidas por satélites de comunicação tradicionais, que normalmente ficam muito mais distantes da Terra e existem em número bem menor.

A internet via satélite é relativamente fácil de usar, e a velocidade da conexão chama a atenção. Os satélites do Starlink orbitam a Terra entre 328 e 614 quilômetros de altitude, uma distância significativamente menor do que a dos satélites dos concorrentes.

Starshield é a unidade de negócios da SpaceX que desenvolve sistemas de satélites para uso militar e de inteligência por governos e forças armadas. Seus principais clientes são órgãos dos EUA, como o Departamento de Defesa (Pentágono), a Space Force e o National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), responsável pelos satélites de reconhecimento do país.

Equipamento da Starlink, empresa de Elon Musk, exposta na Agrishow 2023 em Ribeirão Preto, SP — Foto: Érico Andrade/g1

Os serviços de comunicação segura do Starshield utilizam sistemas avançados de proteção de dados e equipamentos próprios, mas têm como base os satélites do Starlink. Além disso, a empresa afirma que o sistema militar permite observar a Terra e incorporar sensores ou outros equipamentos aos satélites.

O principal cliente é o Pentágono, que gastou bilhões de dólares em serviços do Starlink e do Starshield. Também adquiriu satélites Starshield, incluindo equipamentos de comunicação destinados a detectar antecipadamente possíveis ataques com mísseis, além de uma rede de satélites de espionagem para o NRO, segundo informou a Reuters em 2024.

O sistema Starshield utiliza a rede Starlink para transmitir dados e também conta com satélites próprios. As informações do Starshield podem passar pelos satélites convencionais da Starlink, mas recebem uma camada adicional de criptografia e são mantidas separadas dos dados dos usuários civis.

Para missões de reconhecimento e comunicação militar, há satélites Starshield exclusivos, que não podem ser acessados por clientes civis. Em solo, o sistema também conta com equipamentos próprios para conexão via satélite.

No entanto, terminais Starlink podem ser adaptados para uso do Starshield, como ocorreu na Ucrânia.

Dúvidas sobre a relação entre Starlink e Starshield persistem desde que a Rússia ameaçou, em 2022, satélites ocidentais usados no apoio à Ucrânia.

A SpaceX apresentou o Starshield no final daquele ano, mas o sigilo em torno de programas espaciais ligados à segurança nacional dos EUA tornou difícil determinar com precisão onde termina um sistema e começa o outro.

Essas diferenças tornaram-se motivo de disputa no início deste ano, quando Pentágono e SpaceX entraram em conflito por causa dos preços mais altos dos serviços de satélite utilizados por drones militares durante o conflito com o Irã, segundo a Reuters.

A SpaceX argumentou que alguns clientes, que pagavam cerca de 5 mil dólares por um terminal Starlink, deveriam utilizar o Starshield, a um custo de aproximadamente 25 mil dólares por terminal.

Em 24 de fevereiro de 2022, logo no início da invasão russa, um ataque cibernético atribuído à Rússia tirou do ar a rede de satélites KA-SAT, operada pela empresa americana Viasat. Com isso, as Forças Armadas ucranianas perderam um importante canal de comunicação.

A ajuda aos ucranianos veio do espaço: dias depois, o então ministro da Defesa da Ucrânia, Mykhailo Fedorov, pediu a Musk, pelo Twitter (hoje X), que liberasse o serviço da Starlink no país. Musk respondeu pela mesma rede social: “O serviço Starlink está agora ativo, mais terminais estão a caminho”.

Os serviços oferecidos pela SpaceX acabaram se tornando a espinha dorsal das comunicações da Ucrânia na linha de frente. Os terminais de internet via satélite da empresa de Musk são essenciais para orientar ataques com drones ucranianos de longo alcance nas regiões do sul e do leste do país ocupadas pela Rússia. Essas operações têm causado sérios danos à logística russa.

A Ucrânia recebeu mais de 50 mil terminais Starlink de seus parceiros. A maioria deles, 29.500, é custeada pela Polônia, que paga cerca de 50 milhões de dólares por ano pelas assinaturas do serviço, segundo o ministro do Exterior, Radoslaw Sikorski.

Nas regiões do leste da Ucrânia, onde boa parte da infraestrutura foi destruída, a Starlink é o principal meio de acesso à internet para civis e militares.

Além disso, em 2023, os Estados Unidos, por meio do US European Command, financiaram 500 terminais Starshield por aproximadamente 40 milhões de dólares. Em agosto de 2024, um novo contrato do Space Systems Command ampliou o acesso ao Starshield para 2.500 terminais Starlink que já estavam em uso no país.

Isso ajuda a explicar a confusão entre Starlink e Starshield nas declarações das autoridades ucranianas. Muitas vezes, o equipamento visível no campo de batalha é a antena plana da Starlink. A conexão, porém, pode estar vinculada a outro contrato, com um nível diferente de proteção dos dados e regras próprias.

Os soldados continuam chamando o sistema de Starlink, embora, nesses casos, o serviço seja o Starshield.

articles.title: Educação e sustentabilidade: satélite e horta inovam em escolas | G1
articles.standfirst: Iniciativas envolvem estudantes em atividades práticas, desde o cultivo de alimentos orgânicos destinados à merenda escolar em Jundiaí até o desenvolvimento de um satélite para monitorar a poluição atmosférica em Itapetininga.
articles.summary: Educação e sustentabilidade nas escolas de SP envolvem alunos no cultivo de hortas orgânicas em Jundiaí e na criação de um satélite em Itapetininga.
articles.body:
Um projeto da Prefeitura de Jundiaí (SP) utiliza o cultivo de alimentos orgânicos para ensinar educação ambiental a crianças da rede de ensino. A iniciativa Vale Verde, que existe há quase 30 anos no município, mantém uma horta com aproximadamente 50 mil metros quadrados, onde são produzidos alimentos destinados à merenda escolar.

No local, crianças de 4 a 11 anos aprendem, na prática, como os alimentos são cultivados e qual é a importância de preservar a natureza. As atividades acontecem ao ar livre, entre os canteiros, e aproximam os estudantes do processo de produção dos alimentos que chegam à mesa.

O cultivo é realizado sem o uso de agrotóxicos sintéticos e fertilizantes químicos, seguindo práticas de produção orgânica que contribuem para a conservação do solo e da água.

Em Jundiaí, os alimentos cultivados na horta vão direto para merenda — Foto: TV TEM/ Reprodução

A horta produz mais de 120 mil pés de hortaliças por ano, distribuídos em 26 variedades de alimentos. Entre os produtos cultivados estão cenoura, alface e tomate, além de plantas alimentícias não convencionais (PANCs), como azedinha e vinagreira.

Essas plantas, muitas vezes pouco conhecidas ou confundidas com mato, também fazem parte das atividades educativas. Os alunos têm a oportunidade de conhecer diferentes espécies, entender suas características e ampliar o conhecimento sobre alimentação saudável.

A produção abastece a merenda escolar, permitindo que os estudantes acompanhem parte do caminho percorrido pelos alimentos, desde o cultivo até o prato.

Além de contribuir para a alimentação dos alunos, o projeto busca estimular hábitos mais conscientes desde os primeiros anos de vida.

Ao participar das atividades na horta, as crianças aprendem sobre a origem dos alimentos, a importância da agricultura sustentável e os cuidados necessários para preservar os recursos naturais.

Verduras cultivadas na horta complementam a merenda na escola em Jundiaí — Foto: TV TEM/ Reprodução

Alunos de Itapetininga desenvolvem satélite para medir poluição

Em Itapetininga (SP), estudantes do terceiro ano do ensino médio do Sesi desenvolveram um equipamento para ajudar pesquisadores a monitorar a qualidade do ar. Batizado de ECOsat, o dispositivo tem formato cúbico, com cerca de 10 centímetros de lado, e foi projetado para coletar dados atmosféricos em grandes altitudes.

O projeto reúne conhecimentos de tecnologia, programação e sustentabilidade e tem como objetivo contribuir para o estudo dos níveis de poluição no estado de São Paulo.

Um dos estudantes responsáveis pela iniciativa, Luigi Barros Rechinelli, explica que o equipamento será levado à estratosfera por um balão, que pode alcançar aproximadamente 30 quilômetros de altitude.

Durante o percurso, o ECOsat fará leituras e armazenará os dados em um cartão de memória. Depois que o balão estourar, o equipamento deverá retornar ao solo por meio de um paraquedas. A equipe pretende recuperar o dispositivo para acessar as informações coletadas.

Os dados poderão auxiliar pesquisas sobre a presença de gases de efeito estufa na atmosfera e contribuir para a compreensão das condições ambientais em diferentes localidades.

Alunos do Sesi de Itapetininga participaram do projeto — Foto: TV TEM/ Reprodução

Projeto surgiu durante pesquisas sobre sustentabilidade

O desenvolvimento do ECOsat começou no ano passado, durante atividades de pesquisa com estudantes do último ano do curso técnico em Desenvolvimento de Sistemas. A sustentabilidade foi escolhida como tema para orientar o trabalho.

O professor Rodrigo Raffa, responsável pela orientação do projeto, destaca que a experiência permite aos alunos desenvolver habilidades que podem ser importantes para a carreira profissional.

"São habilidades que no futuro vão fazer a diferença pra aquele funcionário que tem conhecimento dessa área. Saber programar um satélite pode gerar oportunidade pra programar outros projetos e resolver problemas da sociedade "

A proposta combina conhecimentos adquiridos em sala de aula com desafios práticos de engenharia e programação, aproximando os estudantes de áreas como a exploração espacial e o monitoramento ambiental.

Satélite desenvolvido pelos alunos monitora o ar em SP — Foto: TV TEM/ Reprodução

O desempenho do equipamento levou a equipe a participar de duas competições. Na Olimpíada Brasileira de Satélites, os estudantes conquistaram o quinto lugar. Já na Copa Online de Astronáutica, o grupo ficou em primeiro lugar.

Para os participantes, os resultados representam não apenas o reconhecimento do trabalho desenvolvido, mas também a oportunidade de deixar um legado para a escola.

Livia de Gões Rocha, de 18 anos, uma das estudantes envolvidas no projeto, afirma que a expectativa é que a próxima turma dê continuidade à iniciativa.

"A gente deixou um legado pra escola. sobre os satélites , que é algo novo pra gente. E queremos que a próxima turma continue esse projeto e a gente possa auxiliar esses alunos."

A expectativa dos estudantes é realizar o lançamento do ECOsat no próximo ano, quando uma nova equipe deverá assumir a continuidade do trabalho.

Até lá, o projeto representa uma oportunidade de aprofundar os estudos e compartilhar o conhecimento adquirido durante o desenvolvimento do equipamento.

articles.title: Por que Manaus está coberta de fumaça há semanas? Entenda o avanço dos incêndios no Amazonas | G1
articles.standfirst: Capital amazonense registrou episódios de fumaça desde o início de setembro, e o cenário se agravou em outubro. Incêndios alcançaram comunidades, destruíram áreas de floresta e levaram 36 municípios a entrar em situação de emergência.
articles.summary: Capital amazonense registrou episódios de fumaça desde o início de setembro, e o cenário se agravou em outubro. Incêndios alcançaram comunidades, destruíram áreas de floresta e levaram 36 municípios a entrar em situação de emergência.
articles.body:
Em pouco mais de um mês, Manaus teve 19 episódios de fumaça provocada por incêndios florestais. O problema, registrado pela primeira vez em 8 de setembro , se agravou em outubro, quando a capital passou nove dias consecutivos com fumaça no ar, aulas foram suspensas, atividades ao ar livre foram canceladas e centenas de pessoas procuraram atendimento médico por problemas relacionados à poluição .

A fumaça que encobriu a capital vem de incêndios registrados na Região Metropolitana de Manaus e em municípios do interior do Amazonas. O avanço das chamas é favorecido pela vegetação seca, pela baixa umidade e pelas altas temperaturas, em um cenário associado aos efeitos do fenômeno climático El Niño. A ação humana, responsável por iniciar grande parte dos incêndios, também contribui para agravar a situação.

O problema não se limita a Manaus. Entre 1º de setembro e 14 de outubro, o Amazonas registrou 5.365 focos de incêndio, segundo o Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Inpe), um aumento de 195% em relação ao mesmo período de 2025. Em 10 de outubro, o governo estadual decretou situação de emergência em 36 dos 62 municípios do estado , medida reconhecida pelo governo federal no mesmo dia.

Como a fumaça dos incêndios chega a Manaus?

Os incêndios florestais liberam grandes quantidades de fumaça, que contém partículas capazes de prejudicar a saúde. Transportadas pelas correntes de vento, essas partículas podem percorrer dezenas ou centenas de quilômetros e alcançar áreas distantes dos focos de fogo.

Mesmo quando as chamas estão concentradas em municípios do interior, a fumaça pode encobrir Manaus e outras cidades da região.

“Por isso, uma cidade pode ficar coberta de fumaça mesmo sem muitos focos por perto: ela recebe a fumaça emitida em outras áreas, somada à que é produzida localmente”, afirmou o meteorologista Leonardo Vergasta.

Imagem da NASA revela extensão da fumaça sobre Manaus e o AM no dia 9 de outubro em meio ao avanço de queimadas. — Foto: Reprodução/Nasa Worldwide View

A intensidade do problema foi registrada pela plataforma internacional IQAir. Entre 8 e 12 de outubro, Manaus ficou cinco dias consecutivos com a pior qualidade do ar entre as capitais brasileiras , com índices que variaram entre as categorias "insalubre" e "perigoso". No dia 9, a capital chegou a 366 pontos na escala US AQI+, classificação considerada perigosa.

🔎 Segundo a escala US AQI+, a qualidade do ar é considerada boa quando o nível de poluição atmosférica está entre 0 e 50 pontos.

A sequência de dias com fumaça também mudou a rotina dos moradores.

A promotora de vendas Milena Sampaio, que tem asma, passou a semana usando máscara e relatou dificuldades para trabalhar.

"Eu estou com muita falta de ar, muita dor no meu peito. Eu já tenho esse problema de asma, sinusite, rinite e parece que está piorando mais esses dias. Vai fazer uma semana que eu estou muito ruim"

O problema também afetou quem pratica atividades físicas. O estudante Ryan, por exemplo, deixou de jogar futebol e correr por causa da fumaça. "Jogo bola, faço caminhada, de vez em quando vou pra academia também, ai dei uma paradinha agora por conta da fumaça."

O aposentado Veridiana Padeira de Araújo também relatou ter passado mal durante a madrugada e disse não entender por que a situação piorava naquele período do dia.

"Duas, três vezes, de madrugada, quando ela (fumaça) ataca muito, não sei porque", afirmou.

Aposentado Veridiano Araújo reclamou da dificuldade para dormir por causa da fumaça em Manaus. — Foto: Rede Amazônica

Os efeitos chegaram aos serviços de saúde. Entre 1º de julho e 9 de outubro, 375 pessoas foram atendidas em Serviços de Pronto Atendimento (SPAs) de Manaus por problemas relacionados à fumaça, segundo a Secretaria de Estado de Saúde do Amazonas (SES-AM). Desse total, 82 atendimentos ocorreram em apenas uma semana, entre 1º e 8 de outubro .

A rotina da cidade também foi afetada. Em 9 de outubro, a Prefeitura de Manaus suspendeu as aulas da rede municipal de ensino devido à piora da qualidade do ar. No dia seguinte, anunciou o cancelamento de atividades ao ar livre previstas para os dias 11 e 12 . Em 14 de outubro, novas suspensões atingiram programas esportivos e aulas de corrida e natação para adultos.

Depois de nove dias consecutivos de piora, a fumaça chegou a perder força na capital , mas na manhã de sexta-feira (16), voltou a se intensificar nas primeiras horas do dia.

Incêndios florestais avançam pelo Amazonas

O avanço do fogo no estado aparece nos números e nos relatos de quem vive perto das áreas atingidas. Além da fumaça que chega a Manaus, incêndios de grandes proporções destruíram vegetação, ameaçaram territórios indígenas e obrigaram famílias a deixar suas casas .

Um dos principais focos está na região do Rio Urubu, em Itacoatiara. Até 15 de outubro, o incêndio permanecia ativo havia mais de 40 dias . O monitoramento por satélite apontava mais de 3 mil hectares de área destruída, e as chamas já haviam atingido parte do território indígena do povo Mura.

Na Terra Indígena Paraná do Arauató, moradores relataram a morte de animais silvestres e problemas de saúde provocados pela fumaça . A cacica da Aldeia Paricá, Aldenora Maquinez Lima, que também atua como agente indígena de saúde, disse acompanhar os impactos sobre a floresta e a população.

"Dá pena de ver os bichos morrer. Preguiça, pássaros que vão fugindo do fogo e vão se acabando", relatou à Rede Amazônica.

Segundo ela, a fumaça provoca tosse seca e alergias, principalmente entre idosos e pessoas com problemas de saúde. A cacica também afirmou que o fogo se espalha com mais facilidade nas áreas próximas aos lagos, que ficam mais secos durante a estiagem.

Outro incêndio atingiu a região do Lago do Canaçari , também em Itacoatiara. O fogo queimou cerca de 1,3 mil hectares ao longo de aproximadamente 20 dias e foi considerado controlado em 9 de outubro. No dia 13, porém, novos focos de calor foram identificados na mesma região.

O pescador Antônio Miranda, que mora nas proximidades, acompanha diariamente o avanço das chamas para impedir que o fogo alcance a área onde o gado se alimenta.

"Todo dia eu estou indo, pra ver se não passa fogo pra cá, pro campo. Essa é minha luta", contou.

Na Região Metropolitana, outro incêndio atingiu uma área de floresta entre os quilômetros 3 e 4 da rodovia AM-070, em Cacau Pirêra , distrito de Iranduba. Entre 30 de setembro e 2 de outubro, as chamas destruíram cerca de 456 hectares.

Em Manaus, um incêndio em uma área de mata usada para descarte de lixo no Distrito Industrial II atingiu 15 mil metros quadrados, segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros Militar do Amazonas (CBMAM). O fogo contribuiu para a fumaça que encobriu a capital entre 6 e 8 de outubro. Segundo a corporação, foi o primeiro incêndio registrado na cidade a contar com apoio de aeronaves de combate ao fogo .

A proximidade das chamas com áreas residenciais também obrigou famílias a deixar suas casas. Em Careiro da Várzea, moradores precisaram sair de suas residências entre 10 e 11 de outubro, depois que um incêndio se aproximou de uma área habitada. Parte das famílias foi levada temporariamente para uma escola; outras ficaram na casa de vizinhos, segundo a Defesa Civil municipal.

Fumaça encobre cidades e queimadas deixam rastro de destruição no Amazonas

Seca, El Niño e ação humana agravam os incêndios

A quantidade de incêndios ocorre em um período de condições ambientais que favorecem a propagação do fogo. A vegetação mais seca, a baixa umidade do ar e do solo e as temperaturas elevadas facilitam o avanço das chamas. O fenômeno climático El Niño pode agravar esse cenário ao alterar os padrões de chuva e temperatura na região

Segundo a meteorologista Andrea Ramos, períodos prolongados de pouca chuva reduzem a umidade da vegetação e do solo. Com isso, o fogo se espalha com mais facilidade, e a fumaça pode permanecer por mais tempo na atmosfera.

O El Niño, no entanto, não provoca incêndios diretamente. O fenômeno aumenta as condições favoráveis à seca e ao calor, mas o fogo depende de uma fonte de ignição, que pode estar relacionada à ação humana.

A suspeita de incêndios provocados deliberadamente também passou a ser investigada por órgãos ambientais. Durante um sobrevoo em áreas atingidas, em 11 de outubro, o ministro do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima, João Paulo Capobianco, afirmou ter identificado focos de fogo no interior de áreas de floresta preservada, distantes de áreas agropecuárias.

Em Itacoatiara, a Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente informou que 15 pessoas foram autuadas sob suspeita de provocar incêndios florestais. As multas aplicadas ultrapassam R$ 300 mil. Os casos foram encaminhados ao Ministério Público do Amazonas e à Polícia Civil.

Governos ampliam ações de combate ao fogo

Com o agravamento da crise, uma comitiva do governo federal chegou a Manaus em 10 de outubro para acompanhar a situação e reforçar o combate aos incêndios. A equipe reuniu representantes dos ministérios do Meio Ambiente e da Integração e do Desenvolvimento Regional, além de integrantes do Ibama e da Defesa Civil Nacional.

Na mesma data, 11 aeronaves foram mobilizadas para apoiar as operações: seis aviões Air Tractor, um cargueiro KC-390 da Força Aérea Brasileira, três helicópteros do Ibama e um avião Caravan. Também foram mobilizados 290 brigadistas federais.

As aeronaves passaram a atuar em diferentes regiões do estado . Os aviões partem da Base Aérea de Manaus para municípios como Autazes, Itacoatiara e Parintins. Os helicópteros são usados no transporte de brigadistas e equipamentos, enquanto o Caravan presta apoio logístico. Uma base de apoio às operações aéreas também está sendo estruturada em Itacoatiara.

O governo estadual, por sua vez, lançou em maio a operação Amazonas+Verde, que reúne ações de combate a incêndios, fiscalização de crimes ambientais e educação ambiental. Em setembro, publicou um decreto que proibiu o uso do fogo por 120 dias em todo o Amazonas e instituiu o Plano Estadual de Prevenção e Controle do Desmatamento e Queimadas.

articles.title: Senegal-sized Antarctic glacier melting faster than thought: Why it matters
articles.summary: Thwaites glacier has been losing ice for decades. Now there are concerns of rapidly accelerating loss.
articles.body:
The world’s largest glacier is melting much faster and could add twice as much to global sea levels as previously expected over the next century.

New research published this week by a team of glaciologists has found that the Thwaites glacier in West Antarctica is losing mass rapidly because warm seawater is pushing underneath it and melting its core. This could add 1.2 inches (30mm) to water levels even if global warming does not accelerate as predicted.

The findings, published in the journal Nature Communications, add to a growing body of evidence that shows that the glacier, which has been receding for decades, is now losing mass even faster than scientists thought.

Researchers at the University of California in the United States collaborated with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory for the study. Here’s what we know about the findings:

What is Thwaites and why is it important?

Nicknamed the “Doomsday Glacier”, Thwaites is the largest glacier on Earth, spanning an area of around 192,000sq km (74,130sq miles) or roughly the size of Senegal – and larger than the US state of Florida.

It is located on the Walgreen Coast of Marie Byrd Land in remote western Antarctica and forms part of the great West Antarctic ice sheet, which includes other glaciers and is 14 times the size of Thwaites.

The glacier was first mapped in 1947 and is named after the late American glaciologist Fredrik T Thwaites, although he never visited it.

In the 1980s, scientists discovered that Thwaites is melting rapidly and have closely monitored its melting process as concerns have grown ever since.

Because it is so big, the glacier’s collapse would sharply raise global sea levels by a catastrophic amount – although researchers don’t project that will happen for many decades, or even a few centuries.

Together, Thwaites and other glaciers such as the Pine Island glacier – an ice stream in West Antarctica which flows into Pine Island Bay in the Amundsen Sea – act as a barrier that holds back the vast and vulnerable West Antarctic ice sheet. If melted, the ice sheet could cause many coastal cities to be submerged around the world.

At present, ice loss from Thwaites contributes around four percent of all global sea-level rise. Studies have calculated that the glacier has lost more than 1,000 billion tonnes of ice since 2000, and continues to lose 50 billion tonnes of ice per year.

The main drivers are warm ocean water which is actively melting the Thwaites glacier from underneath it, according to several studies.

Ocean warming is caused by human-induced climate change, in particular from the burning of polluting fossil fuels.

In a 2019 study, the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory discovered a giant underwater cavity beneath the Thwaites glacier that spread across an area two-thirds the size of Manhattan, which researchers said was likely speeding up the glacier’s thinning.

Rising temperatures have caused glaciers to lose about five percent of their ice since 2000, according to the European Space Agency.

Thwaites could add as much as 1.2 inches (30mm) – double the current estimates – to sea levels by 2100, even without any additional global warming, the study found.

The researchers said they used new computer models that paint a clearer picture of melting activity under the threatened glacier at its grounding line – the boundary where it transitions from resting entirely on bedrock to spreading out over the sea in the form of ice shelves.

Where other ice sheet models conclude a grounding line is fixed, the scientists said they developed the concept of a broader “grounding zone” instead. In this scenario, seawater lifts and lowers the ice in a “tidal pumping” process that allows warm water to reach “deep underneath the ice sheets and causing vigorous melting,” lead author Mattia Poinelli, a project scientist at UCLA, told media.

That melting process is accelerating the Thwaites’ “unpinning” from the Mouginot Ridge – an important underwater bedrock currently stabilising the glacier from below. The study concluded that there is a 60 percent chance that Thwaites could unpin from the ridge by the end of the century.

However, experts say more studies are needed to accurately predict the volume of Thwaites’ ice loss.

In separate findings, scientists from the British Antarctic Survey concluded that Thwaites will continue losing ice for at least the next 150 years, even under the most extreme ocean cooling conditions imaginable.

The study, which used computer simulation models that examined the melting effects of the ocean over the next century and a half, was published in Geophysical Research Letters in July.

articles.title: Dozens of venomous snakes were spotted inside an Australian airport, including a Qantas lounge; catchers say they appeared almost everywhere-from passenger areas to offices
articles.summary: An airport in central Australia is preparing for its summer snake season after reports of dozens of sightings around its terminal, including inside an
articles.body: An airport in central Australia is preparing for its summer snake season after reports of dozens of sightings around its terminal, including inside an airline lounge and staff offices. According to reports by Kids News and the NT News, snake catcher Rex Neindorf has removed several reptiles from Alice Springs Airport, prompting renewed attention to how wildlife can enter busy public spaces as temperatures rise. Airport operator Airport Development Group (ADG) says it is monitoring areas of concern and has arrangements in place for professional snake removal.Why snakes are entering the airportThe sightings are linked to the extreme summer heat of Australia’s Northern Territory, where snakes seek shade and shelter during the hottest parts of the day. Buildings can provide cooler spaces and potential hiding places, making airport interiors attractive to reptiles moving through the surrounding landscape.Conservation biologist Chris Jolly, an adjunct research fellow at Charles Darwin University, explained in the Kids News report that snakes do not distinguish between natural habitats and human-built structures. If a building offers shelter, water or access to prey, it can become a suitable place for them to explore.The sightings do not necessarily indicate a sudden increase in the local snake population. Seasonal weather conditions can make snakes more active at certain times, increasing the likelihood of encounters with people. In Central Australia, their activity may shift towards the cooler evening and night hours when daytime temperatures become particularly intense.Snakes have appeared in passenger and staff areasLocal snake catcher Rex Neindorf said his team had removed reptiles from several parts of Alice Springs Airport, including departure and arrival entrances, passenger check-in areas and the Qantas lounge. He also described incidents involving two western brown snakes found inside the terminal, one in a public area and another in an office used by airport employees.Western brown snakes are highly venomous and can pose a serious risk if approached or provoked. Neindorf has also encountered whip snakes around the airport, which are generally considered less dangerous than western brown snakes but should still be left alone.The reports have raised concerns about the possibility of encounters in areas used by large numbers of travellers. However, Neindorf said he was not aware of any snake-related injuries at the airport, either inside the terminal or on its grounds.Airport steps up monitoring as temperatures riseADG, which manages Alice Springs Airport as well as Darwin and Tennant Creek airports, has begun monitoring locations where snakes are more likely to appear as the weather warms. The company has also said it uses warning signs to alert passengers and calls trained snake catchers when reptiles need to be removed.Neindorf has previously provided snake-safety training to airport employees, helping staff recognise potential hazards and respond appropriately. The airport’s approach focuses on monitoring, awareness and professional relocation rather than allowing workers or passengers to handle the animals themselves.The airport is located in a region where encounters with snakes are a recurring seasonal concern. Alice Springs Town Council advises residents who spot a snake to maintain a safe distance and contact a professional catcher. Its guidance also warns against approaching or attempting to capture reptiles, even when their species is uncertain.How travellers can stay safeAuthorities and wildlife specialists advise people to avoid approaching snakes, attempting to move them or blocking their escape routes. Anyone who spots a snake inside the airport should alert airport staff and keep other passengers away from the area.For now, the reported sightings highlight a seasonal challenge for a facility operating in the middle of Australia’s arid landscape. As temperatures climb, airport staff will need to remain alert to the possibility of reptiles entering buildings, while ensuring that passengers can move safely through the terminal.

articles.title: In 2019, researchers shifted the blades of an eggbeater-shaped vertical turbine; wind-tunnel tests found its peak power coefficient rose about 10%
articles.summary: In 2019, researchers enhanced the power coefficient of an eggbeater-shaped vertical-axis wind turbine by shifting blade positions, resulting in a significant efficiency improvement during wind-tunnel tests.
articles.body: Wind turbine designers often look for ways to generate more electricity without increasing the size of a machine or adding more material. Sometimes, improving performance depends on changing how the blades are arranged rather than building a larger rotor. In 2019, scientists tested the performance of an eggbeater-type vertical-axis wind turbine by adjusting the position of the blades of the turbine. In wind tunnel experiments, the modified turbine reached a peak power coefficient about 10% higher than the unmodified version of the same turbine, under the conditions tested.Researchers compared three Darrieus turbine configurationsHilewit and colleagues published Power Coefficient Measurements of a Novel Vertical Axis Wind Turbine in Energy Science & Engineering in 2019, studying how changing the positions of the blades influenced the efficiency of a Darrieus vertical axis wind turbine. In a Darrieus turbine, the blades are curved and rotate around a vertical axis, which gives the turbine the look of an egg beater. This type of turbine has an advantage over traditional designs because there is no need to turn it towards the wind.The researchers compared a conventional turbine with two modified configurations called the 50% shifted troposkien-shape vertical-axis wind turbine (50% STS-VAWT) and the 100% shifted version (100% STS-VAWT). Wind-tunnel tests used three 2-bladed models built with the same height, swept area, chord, and NACA0015 airfoil, run at 600 and 700 rpm with tip-speed ratios of about 2 to 6, as described in the National Research Council Canada’s copy of the study. The research team sought to find out how blade position affected aerodynamic performance, in particular blade-vortex interaction. Whenever a blade moves through air, it leaves a wake of disturbed air, and a following blade can pass through that disturbance, which affects how the blades move.The 50% shifted design achieved a higher peak power coefficientBased on the wind tunnel tests, it was established that the 50% shifted design outperformed the conventional turbine under the given testing conditions. At 600 rpm, and correcting for wind tunnel blockage, the 50% shifted turbine reached a maximum power coefficient of 0.23, while the conventional design reached 0.21. That is a relative increase of about 10%, or 0.02 in absolute terms. The authors link the improvement to a reduction in blade-vortex interaction. At 700 rpm the 50% shifted design also showed a higher peak power coefficient than both other designs, and the study reports this held with or without the blockage correction. The results indicate that blade position can affect how effectively a vertical-axis turbine captures wind energy.Shifting the blades further did not improve performanceThis experiment shows that blade displacement alone does not guarantee better results. The design engineers have to take into account the interactions between blade shape, rotor dimensions, and speed of operation. First, the conclusions were based on tests performed on small turbines in a wind tunnel.Additionally, the study reports an uncertainty of about 5.4% for the corrected peak power coefficient of the 50% shifted turbine at 600 rpm and about 3.7% for the tip-speed ratio, at a 95% confidence level. The 100% shift setup did not yield the same benefit as the 50% shift setup. At 600 rpm, the study found it had similar efficiency to the conventional turbine at lower and higher tip-speed ratios and lower efficiency around the peak power.Further testing is needed before commercial applicationThe 2019 experiment found that a 50% blade shift could raise the peak power coefficient without enlarging the rotor’s swept area. That does not mean every turbine using this arrangement will produce 10% more power outdoors, since wind conditions and structural requirements also affect performance. Physical tests on larger machines would be needed to show whether the design delivers consistently better results in real conditions. For turbine manufacturers, the key conclusion is that blade position matters to turbine performance.

articles.title: Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers
articles.summary: The Apple HomeView’s simplified, hands-free instructions strip out much of what’s essential to online recipes.
articles.body: When Apple revealed the HomeView to the world, it did so with an unusual ad for the company: Instead of pristine, polished tech in immaculate rooms, it’s a three-minute look at the messy, frantic morning routine of a family of five. Apple’s new smart display sits in the center of the chaos on the kitchen table, helping the family check their calendars, send messages, and pull up a French toast recipe in seconds, with simple, step-by-step instructions. The HomeView is just the latest in a long line of websites, browser extensions, and smart home gadgets with the same promise: that it can take an online recipe and strip it down to the essentials. Instead of scrolling a lengthy webpage that might range from helpful cooking instructions to seemingly irrelevant personal anecdotes, with the recipe itself way down at the bottom, you simply get ingredient lists, cooking instructions, and timers, all navigable hands-free with voice controls and Siri AI. No distractions, no unnecessary text, and no need to deal with a touchscreen while you’re wrist-deep in a chicken carcass. The appeal is obvious. There’s only one group of people likely to object: the food writers who created those recipes in the first place. I would know, since I’m one of them — I have my own food newsletter where I occasionally publish recipes, so I have a little skin in the game. The problem is that converting a recipe into easy-to-follow instructions in Apple’s own format also strips it of its context, including the ads and affiliate links that many recipe writers rely on for their income. Recipes may often be free to read, but they’re not free to create, and solutions like Apple’s remove the main ways websites and writers recoup those costs. “Tools that just extract the recipe,” Eater senior reporter Bettina Makalintal says, “break apart that unspoken social contract with recipe developers and audiences.” [Image: Apple pitches the HomeView as a hands-free cooking assistant. The online recipe landscape is a diverse place. Behemoths like Allrecipes and NYT Cooking host tens of thousands of recipes each, some from professional chefs and others from home cooks. Countless dedicated food publications run original recipe content, and thousands of independent chefs produce their own, across blogs, newsletters, YouTube accounts, and TikTok pages. While much of the writing on a recipe page may get on budding cooks’ nerves — we’ve all heard the jokes about being forced to read someone’s grandma’s life story before getting to their cookie recipe — it’s there for a reason. For one thing, it’s usually the only part of a recipe that a writer can copyright — the rest is regarded as mere instructions. But that extra writing is also there because before it worked so hard to strip the text out, Big Tech insisted on it. “Recipe writers needed to pad out the text in a certain way so that their recipes would have a chance of coming up in a Google search,” Makalintal explains. The good news for recipe writers is that Apple’s approach guarantees at least one visit to their original web page. To load a recipe onto the HomeView screen you have to first open it either on your iPhone or through Safari on the HomeView itself, ensuring you’ll see its ads at least once. That’s welcome, but for website owners it’s still a lot less valuable than the repeated ad impressions that come from someone scrolling down the page and staying on it while they cook. "“Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll. So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.”" - Jaya Saxena It’s not just bad for the writers, either — readers and home cooks may be missing out too. “The additional information around recipes can sometimes be really helpful when it comes to troubleshooting problems that could come up while cooking or addressing things like ingredient swaps,” says Makalintal. Apple’s simplified steps may make some recipes easier to follow, but others might become harder without crucial context included elsewhere on the page. And as common as gripes about recipe intros are, they’ve long been easy to skip if you really insist. “Nearly every food blog has a ‘jump to recipe’ button right up at the top, so you don’t actually have to scroll,” says Jaya Saxena, one of the founder-owners of the food website Ravenous. “So if you’re still out here complaining about these essays, you’re just an asshole.” [Image: Amazon’s Echo Show devices have long had similar recipe features, but powered by partner publishers. Apple is far from the first company to attempt to streamline online recipes. In 2021 startup Recipeasly promised to “fix” online recipes by removing the ads and “life stories.” It barely lasted a weekend before online backlash forced its founders to take it offline. Bigger tech companies have been able to plow through that resistance. Amazon’s Echo Show displays offer similar hands-free cooking features to the HomeView’s, though only with partner sites like Allrecipes or Epicurious. Google’s Nest Hubs used to as well, though Google ultimately removed the step-by-step recipe feature from its Nest Hubs in 2024, along with other “underutilized” features. Apple’s approach, which it says will work with any online recipe that uses Google’s search-friendly recipe formatting, is unique among the current smart home hubs. Perhaps most egregious of all, Google Search now uses Gemini AI to amalgamate online recipes, presenting a streamlined version right on the search page, saving users from ever needing to click through to the original sources at all. Saxena says that for established writers, this is “more like a continuation of the threats they’ve already seen.” Unless Apple sells vast quantities of HomeView displays, its recipe function is still likely to be used by far fewer people than Google’s AI search recipes, let alone recipes from other AI assistants and tools, which are also more egregious in how they take advantage of online content. “I would put the threat level below AI summaries,” says Makalintal, because their “opaque” sourcing “really is erasing labor.” Some major recipe platforms might be able to reduce the impact by getting on board. While the HomeView doesn’t have its own app store, it does support casting apps to the screen using the same tech as CarPlay. That means big apps like Allrecipes or NYT Cooking will have the option of presenting content on the HomeView on their own terms. Independent writers are unlikely to be able to do the same. For them, the choice remains as it has for some time: Stick it out with ever-diminishing Google traffic and ad revenue; take on more sponsored content and paid-for recipes with big brands; or move to a paywall or newsletter business model. Smaller recipe developers are turning to Substack, says Makalintal, where it’s easy to lock recipes behind a paywall. I’m one of them — on my newsletter I restrict my recipes to paid subscribers, a reflection of the fact that they’re the most time-consuming articles I publish. I’ve asked Apple how the HomeView recipe tool will handle paywalled recipes, but at the time of publishing haven’t gotten an answer. But the move en masse to newsletter platforms “has led to some subscription fatigue among home cooks,” Makalintal says, and few cooks will start a paid subscription to access a single recipe, suggesting it’s not likely to support the whole industry. Some version of paid-for content may be the only answer going forward, though, for creators both big and small. Tech companies like Apple will have to grapple with how their tools work when access to free content gets trickier, and the rest of us may have to get used to paying for recipes again. “A good, creative recipe that has been tested to ensure it really works takes time and effort and money,” Saxena says. “It is a real skill to communicate how something is made when you’re not physically with that person, and buying all the ingredients needed to test things multiple times is expensive. People should probably be more comfortable paying for that.”

articles.title: SpaceX’s ambitious, expensive gamble to replace AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
articles.summary: Cell service isn’t rocket ships or flying cars, but it could be a booming business for SpaceX.
articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Walter Piecyk, a partner and analyst at LightShed Partners who covers tech, media, and telecom, about SpaceX’s recently announced plan to become a major wireless carrier. Last week, SpaceX agreed to buy a big chunk of low-band spectrum to expand the Starlink network, spectrum that’s been traded around the telecom business for decades now. SpaceX’s ambitious plan is to use that spectrum to help build “the world’s most advanced mobile network.” --- [Image: Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- Combined with news that the FCC approved the deployment of 15,000 next-gen Starlink satellites and the company’s previous agreement to purchase close to $20 billion worth of EchoStar spectrum last year, it’s now clear SpaceX is serious about competing with AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile. I’ve covered the telecom business for a long time, and I’ve always known that these companies can say they want to do something until they run into the harsh reality of how expensive it is to actually do it. The telecom graveyard of pivots, bad ideas, and failed acquisitions is vast. But we know that, just like I mentioned earlier, it could make buying EchoStar make sense because you’re buying effectively cash in your own stock on the cheap. There are different ways to put cash obviously on the balance sheet in $10 or $20 billion chunks. Obviously the structure of these companies — they’re all Elon’s companies in the end, and he’s managed them as closely as anyone can manage big public companies. But to make it as dumb as possible, say you have a dollar and if Gwynne Shotwell has a dollar and she wants to light the dollar on fire, she’ll put it in xAI against some return somewhere that might be $50 trillion total addressable market (TAM) or whatever their prospectus said. Or you could put the dollar into Starlink Mobile in the build-out and you will probably return $1.10. That is what that business looks like because they will get some customers away from AT&T and Verizon. They’re already running that thing profitably. The idea that they need to show some return somewhere, it feels like that’s why they’re making this move. Not because it makes the most financial sense, it just makes the most financial sense in the context of SpaceX. You may be right. The problem with that belief is that it’s going to take time for them to get that dollar of profit out of the mobile business. They still have to build the network. They still have to sign up customers. You’re going to be negative EBITDA for a while. If you have two different businesses and you think the returns are significantly higher or more interesting to your investors to get to that next catalyst for space compute or Optimus or whatever it is, that is going to play a role. What does Elon happen to care about the most at that moment? What is more interesting to him to do? Isn’t space compute a little bit more interesting to allocate those dollars than taking some mobile customers from AT&T? Although the man’s addicted to his phone and I bet he hates seeing that AT&T logo in the corner. There’s just a part of that that’s always with these guys. Let’s talk about the existing telecoms. They do seem a bit panicked. For a time, they were juggernauts. These were unstoppable businesses as mobile was growing. They poured a bunch of money into the 5G transition. I’ve described the telecom industry as a bunch of lobbyists. Boy, did the lobbyists win the 5G transition. Boy, did they collect all the favors and all the capital they could to build out these networks and then reality hit them in the face. We beat China to some kind of network and then the thing that we were supposed to win did not happen. Now we’re doing it again with AI, but that’s a different conversation. But that was the narrative with 5G: If we didn’t beat China to 5G, something. Who knows what, but we got to cut all the corners to build this network and spend all the money. It just didn’t pay off. You’re an analyst, you’re in the trades. I skim the trades and boy are all these CEOs saying, “We’ve got to generate some revenue with these networks now.” You mentioned Mike Sievert is gone, the old CEO of Verizon’s gone. It just didn’t pay off for these guys. Yeah, 5G didn’t deliver. Some of the promises were BS from the beginning. You talked about this earlier regarding autonomous cars. You’re not going to rely on the network to make that millimeter-second decision of whether you’re going to hit the car in front of you or not. Remote surgery, even if that was a thing, how is that a scalable business where you’re generating hundreds of billions of dollars of revenue? These were all silly. Sievert used to be the guy saying, “People would say the same thing about LTE, there’s no application.” That was not even true. If you remember, the application was video and we knew that LTE was going to enable video and that’s exactly what happened. You’re 100 percent right. This was just a way for them to get more spectrum because they were going to still have data growth on their networks. Capturing more spectrum to be able to handle the existing growth, and that’s cheaper to get spectrum, even at tens of billions of dollars, than it is to try and build the network for that capacity. If they had just said, “We’re going to spend all this money and at the end of it, tens of thousands of people will be able to livestream Taylor Swift during the Eras tour on every one of those stops,” Americans would have said, “Go, go faster. Yes, we understand what that is.” That is truly the thing they enabled. It’s very cool. It’s millimeter wave in stadiums and that’s cool. I don’t know if there’s another one. That said, they are on their back foot. They did spend a lot of money. This is around the time when, in my history as a journalist, they would start talking about 6G, and they want to, but they know they shouldn’t, so they don’t. They’re having the meetings. They are certainly not as loud about the next round of investment as they would normally be in the cycle. Now they have a competitor. Your analysis is that Verizon is by far the weakest here. They have the most to lose. Explain why that is. One other thing to mention is you have a very active FCC chair that would like to raise, and put on his resume, $100 billion from spectrum auction. You’re right, they’re going to talk about 6G again and have to come up with some type of revenue stream to justify getting this money. It’s going to be a lot harder though. They’re already pretty levered. They’ve got a new competitor. In terms of Verizon, the issue is that AT&T has seen this thing developing for some time. They’ve built a fiber network. There’s only so much that wireless can do where a fiber network is ultimately your best connection. If you think about customers that own fiber and wireless, very high-value, very low-churn customers. That’s been their strategy. They’re plodding along. They’re going to get their two or three percent revenue growth and just pay their dividend and do their thing. That is the standard telco. T-Mobile didn’t have that. They’ve got the dynamics — a lot of politics right now between Deutsche Telekom wanting to own it and not wanting to pay a high price and how that all plays out. Verizon just made a lot of bad strategic bets on spectrum. Obviously, AT&T had their own issues, but at least they got out of DirecTV and Warner quick enough and turned the ship. But Verizon bought millimeter wave spectrum when they could have bought EchoStar and bought spectrum… even now they’re spectrum-constrained compared to their competitors and they need to go out and spend $10–$15 billion on the EchoStar spectrum. You have a new CEO in there who is not really a telco guy who’s just doing his thing, saying, “We’re just going to cut costs.” The EBITDA is going to look good because they’re just firing a bunch of people and there’s going to be a result. There is going to be an impact of firing that many people in the organization. It may appease investors to make the EBITDA look good for the next couple of quarters. But at some point you have to show and have a strategy for some type of revenue growth. What is Verizon’s differentiation in the market right now? They have none. They’re the most in the crosshairs of where SpaceX and even the cable companies can continue to eat away at those customers. That is surprising to me. It’s just my own history. I grew up in the midwest. I went to college in the midwest. That was Cingular territory and it became AT&T. When I moved to New York in 2010, Verizon was the gold standard network in the Northeast. It was the one everyone had. It cost the most money because it was the best network. The iPhone coming to Verizon a couple of years later was a huge deal. Verizon’s network was so powerful at that time that they could try to force the Blackberry Storm down people’s throats. They were confident enough that their network was the thing holding people to them, that that was a worthwhile strategy. Obviously, it didn’t work. They made the wrong bet. You’re saying they made the wrong bet on millimeter wave. They made the wrong bet on other spectrum acquisitions. The one that I’m not quite tracking is media. They did buy a bunch of dumb stuff. At one point they owned Tumblr, which is just one of the most confusing media outcomes of all time. But that stuff was all cheaper and easier for them to flip or shut down than AT&T buying all of Time Warner and putting out a 4:3 black-and-white Justice League movie. How did AT&T survive that? But you’re saying Verizon can’t survive owning Yahoo? That’s a fair pushback, in that the media impact to Verizon was a lot less than AT&T. But these again were separate businesses. Obviously, it was a capital allocation issue for a period of years. But the decisions on the spectrum front and the competitive front, and T-Mobile’s impact, John Legere’s impact in taking away the claim of having the best network, left them in a spot where they basically said, “We’ll just keep increasing price on our customers and we’ll get that 2 or 3 percent revenue growth.” And they just lost the narrative of what they meant to customers. I don’t really think under the new CEO that’s been regained. Do you think their ability to say they have the best network is just gone? That’s completely gone. That’s the crazy thing about this. The networks are effectively commoditized. These networks are basically the same. And they’re getting 60 percent margins. That’s the whole thing with Dish Wireless — even if it wasn’t on their network and you guys tested it, it wasn’t on their network, you could have been buying AT&T’s network at half price. It’s crazy the average revenue per user (ARPU) and the margins that these guys get for what is effectively a commoditized market. That’s why the AT&T strategy is interesting because at least they’re trying to bundle that with a high-value fiber network. But for the other guys, it’s just commoditized wireless. I would actually say the other strategic mistake Verizon made along the way was they got away from Fios. They decided it wasn’t worthwhile. It seems like they’re trying to reinvest in that now and go after that AT&T strategy. Given their lack of spectrum, they can only take fixed wireless so far. You’re right. I wouldn’t be surprised if they got back to investing in fiber. The difference, obviously, with Fios is that you have union issues and a lot of cost structure issues that they were dealing with. But the pivot to doing more fiber and perhaps laying off the fixed wireless, which is straining the network, is probably the right decision for them and what you’ll see happen going forward. I want to end on just a big picture question here. We have covered so many crazy telecom mergers and it always feels like the right answer is to put more competition in the system. We’ve mentioned John Legere several times in this conversation. He only got that job and T-Mobile only got to exist the way it does because AT&T was prevented from buying T-Mobile. They paid a breakup fee, which subsidized a huge portion of that early growth and those early strategic moves that Legere was able to make. But that was good for the market. Consumers got a CEO who tried to change the market and have better customer experiences, reinvested that money in the network. That was good. The existence of Dish Network is T-Mobile trying to buy Sprint and instead of blocking the deal, we imposed some wild structural remedies and Makan Delrahim, who ran antitrust in the first Trump administration, rightly or wrongly engineered the outcome of Dish Network existing. That was Delrahim’s preferred outcome: “We’re going to let this happen, but we need to have four carriers. Charlie Ergen is my guy. We were going to stand up a fourth one.” From my perspective, it just seemed obvious that he was never going to do that. And he didn’t. Maybe I was correct to make that bet, but it just seemed obvious that Dish Network was going to hold onto a bunch of spectrum, watch the prices rise and then flip it when it turned out they never built their network. They had to hit targets with the FCC that they just weren’t hitting over time. Now, we have a true fourth competitor, or at least an aggressive competitor of the market in Elon, who’s probably going to try to actually do this thing and these companies are running scared. Is this just evidence that we should have four carriers in the United States? And that when inevitably Verizon tries to buy T-Mobile, we should just say, no, the right answer is four and we’re not going to go to three again. Under Chairman Wheeler, which goes way back, four was the number. Wheels and I were buds. If you called him now, he’d say, “I told you it should have been four and it’s going to go back there.” Obviously, in the new administration, they didn’t believe that that was the case. You see Chairman Carr pointing to prices, how he sees them being down and the competition that’s happened in fixed wireless. But you always want more competition in a market. It drives innovation and it lowers prices and margins are approaching 60 percent in the wireless business. I can’t say we’ve had a tremendous amount of innovation, which gets back to what the telcos are doing in fear by refusing to give SpaceX a wholesale agreement. That’s their right. But at some point, if the FCC’s mandate is to act in the public interest, we have a current administration — and who knows who gets in during the next administration — but if these telcos are going to push back so hard on what the fourth competitor, in this case SpaceX, is going to do, the FCC can probably get involved in some ways. That is the risk that they run by being so vocally against Elon Musk in the market. You talk about the ultimate consolidation. It’s funny. We should save all these quotes now where they’re saying, “Elon can’t be a competitor because he only has 80 MHz of spectrum.” Because then when they want to merge with someone, they’re going to claim, “No, he’s actually a competitor.” They’re going to deny that as a competitive threat. There’s nothing funnier than a giant telecom insisting that a thing that is not a competitor is their competitor. They all do it. Last question. Again, this is just the big think rattling around my head. We might be on a cusp of an entire paradigm shift in what mobile devices even are. If you look at Meta, they’re going to put up the Muse charm and maybe we’re all going to talk to little cartoon AIs all day that run agents in a data center. Our use of mobile bandwidth to watch video will go down because we’re not even carrying phones anymore. Is that a risk here? Is anybody thinking about this? We think about this every day at LightShed, in terms of all the different ways that AI [exists] and how we interact with our information and how we interact with commerce and using agents. Muse has obviously been something we’ve been waiting for from someone and there’s going to be other versions of that. But you’re right. It could decrease [phone usage], and it’s an Apple risk. It decreases the importance of the status of holding an iPhone if you’re just not interacting with your data in the same way. If that happens, that whole paradigm in terms of the telcos and providing the subsidies changes. Whenever there’s change, there’s an opportunity for disruption and for margins to be contracted. It does change things and maybe SpaceX could play. Elon’s been asked about making a device. I know Qualcomm, when you meet with those guys, says, “We have 40 different guys out there making devices.” I don’t think he’s going to add one more thing to his list, but again, let’s get back to what we’ve talked about during this podcast and narrative. Will Terafab happen? Will data centers in space happen? It may not happen, but you can maybe talk about building a phone and then that becomes one more issue that the telcos have to deal with in terms of dealing with their customers. Why am I using this iPhone when I should be using this completely different device, whether it’s coming from OpenAI or Anthropic or maybe SpaceX? The idea of Elon shipping a mid-range Android phone with the Play Store on it is so deeply funny to me. I truly hope it happens because that’s the product you can make today. Maybe there’s a paradigm shift and there’s a different set of products. But right now you need to have Instagram and there’s really only one path to getting Instagram, which is shipping an Android phone with the Play Store on it. We just saw Amazon essentially capitulate with their new tablets. If you’re focused on the future, you have to concede to the present. I truly do not believe we will see a mid-range Android phone from SpaceX. But you’re saying they might start talking about it. No, I agree with you. I’m just saying when you’re trying to build narratives, why not throw that in the hopper? The bigger issue is someone’s going to build something that may resonate with... We’ve gone a long time. We’re spending $1,000 for these phones that are giving us some basic swipe functionality. They’re going to change in terms of how you use them. This is a bigger and more obvious issue for Apple than anybody else, but it does change how the telcos are going to act and the role that they’re going to play and where that margin should be. They gave up a lot of value to Apple at some point during this continuum of the wireless industry. We’re going through another paradigm change, so we’ll see how those value splits play out. Walter, we’re going to have to have you back soon because it feels like these things are going to happen fast. I was very happy to nerd out about telecom with you. Thanks for being on Decoder. I appreciate it. Thank you. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email! articles.title: Former MIT scientist wins $6M defamation verdict against colleague who accused him of sexual misconduct
articles.summary: David Sabatini won $6 million after a jury found his colleague's sexual harassment claims were defamatory, but the fallout from MIT cost him years.
articles.body: A former Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) scientist won a legal victory this week after losing his position following sexual misconduct allegations made by a female colleague. Dr. David Sabatini, a former MIT biology professor and prominent biomedical researcher, was awarded $6 million in damages Friday after a jury found that his former colleague, Dr. Kristin Knouse, had defamed him. At the time of the allegations, Sabatini had led a research lab at the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for approximately 24 years. His work focused on cell biology and its connections to neurodegenerative diseases, diabetes, aging and cancer. FORMER CAL SOFTBALL PLAYER FILES LAWSUIT AGAINST UNIVERSITY, FEMALE EX-COACH OVER ALLEGED SEXUAL MISCONDUCT In 2021, Sabatini lost his position at Whitehead following an internal investigation into allegations made by Dr. Kristin Knouse, a younger colleague who worked at the institute. The pair met in 2012 and began a sexual relationship in 2018, which ended the following year, according to court documents obtained by Fox News Digital. Knouse later alleged the relationship was coerced. AOC'S DRAMATIC RETELLING OF CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS COLLIDES WITH COMPLAINT DETAILS According to records from the investigation, Whitehead also found that Sabatini had fostered a sexualized atmosphere in his lab. He subsequently resigned from the institute. Following his departure from Whitehead — and amid an ongoing investigation at MIT — Sabatini filed a defamation lawsuit against Knouse, "alleging claims for defamation, tortious interference with contractual, prospective, and advantageous relations," according to court documents. US OLYMPIC HERO NANCY HOGSHEAD WINS LEGAL BATTLE AFTER VOLLEYBALL COACH'S $250M DEFAMATION SUIT IS DISMISSED Knouse subsequently filed a counterclaim against Sabatini, alleging sexual harassment. Throughout the legal battle, Sabatini maintained that he had never fostered an improper atmosphere in his lab and that his relationship with Knouse was consensual. EX-MAYOR FOUND LIABLE FOR ALLEGED SEXUAL ASSAULTS OF 7 WOMEN, ORDERED TO PAY $13M During the trial, his attorney, Lisa Arrowood, cited text messages between the pair that she argued showed Knouse willingly participated in their relationship. In one 2020 exchange, Knouse lamented that she was "pouring a lot of energy and emotion into a game I'm destined to lose" and wondered "if it's best for both of us to cut all but work-related ties for the foreseeable future." FORMER UCLA GYNECOLOGIST SENTENCED AFTER PLEADING GUILTY TO SEXUALLY ASSAULTING PATIENTS AT SCHOOL She concluded the message by writing, "But most times I feel at peace and want to do everything and anything I can to help you." Sabatini and his legal team argued in court that the relationship was consensual. They also presented evidence they said showed that Knouse had become jealous of another woman in whom Sabatini was interested and had sought to have him fired. HARVEY WEINSTEIN SENTENCED TO 15 YEARS IN PRISON FOR 2006 SEX CRIME IN NEW YORK A day after a Suffolk County jury awarded him $6 million in damages, Sabatini told Fox News Digital that hearing the verdict was "overwhelming." "It was done," Sabatini said. "We had won everything, lost nothing. It was like a complete sweep." HOUSE BACKS MASSIE'S PUSH TO RELEASE TAXPAYER-FUNDED SEXUAL HARASSMENT SETTLEMENT RECORDS Five years after filing his lawsuit, Sabatini emerged from the trial with a favorable verdict after the jury rejected Knouse's counterclaims, including her allegation that he had coerced her into a sexual relationship. "The sad reality of our time is that society still has a difficult time believing women and appreciating the difficulty they encounter with men who too often control their fate," Knouse’s attorney, Ellen Zuker, said in a statement to the New York Times. Knouse’s attorney did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment. Despite the legal victory, Sabatini is now attempting to pick up the pieces of his career. The allegations seeped into every aspect of his life, and many of his loved ones — including his parents, nephew and high school-aged son — began receiving threats shortly after Knouse’s claims were made public. "Everyone who came out and tried to defend me got attacked every which way," Sabatini told Fox News Digital. Shortly after his departure from MIT and Whitehead, Sabatini discussed a potential faculty position at New York University (NYU). But after students and faculty members protested his possible hiring in 2022, the university ultimately did not offer him a job. Sabatini said protesters also appeared outside his parents' home, drawing his family further into the controversy. One year later, in 2023, Sabatini landed a job at the Institute of Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry in Prague after receiving several offers from foreign countries — including China. He later opened a Boston branch of the institute, and he splits his time between Prague and the United States. "It was a necessity," Sabatini said. "There were no options [in the United States]. So there was no choice." Following Friday's verdict, Knouse's attorneys said they planned to appeal, while Sabatini's legal team also prepared to challenge the dismissal of his claims against the Whitehead Institute. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "I think institutions don't care about due process," Sabatini said. "They care about having a certain conclusion. And for whatever reason that one could discuss, at that time the conclusion was, ‘Get this guy out of here and make an example of him.’" Sabatini said he hopes to rebuild his life and career following the verdict and eventually return to working primarily in the United States. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "But ultimately for me, it’s just being able to be close to my son before he goes to college," Sabatini told Fox News Digital. "That’s really number one through 100." Fox News Digital also reached out to the Whitehead Institute and MIT for comment.

articles.title: Researchers used drone LiDAR to scan rugged Australian bushland that is difficult to search on foot; the technology led them to three previously unregistered Aboriginal rock shelters with red hand stencils
articles.summary: Researchers have used drone-based laser scanning to identify and document three previously unregistered Aboriginal rock shelters in Australia's Blue
articles.body: Researchers have used drone-based laser scanning to identify and document three previously unregistered Aboriginal rock shelters in Australia's Blue Mountains, revealing traces of cultural heritage in rugged bushland that is difficult to explore on foot. According to the Australian Museum, the research team worked with the Dharug Custodian Aboriginal Corporation to identify potential sites using LiDAR technology. Subsequent field visits confirmed rock shelters containing red hand stencils and stone artefacts. The findings, published in the journal Remote Sensing, highlight how aerial mapping can help Aboriginal communities and archaeologists locate, document and protect cultural heritage that might otherwise remain unrecorded.How drone technology helped locate the sheltersThe research brought together archaeologists from the University of Sydney's Vere Gordon Childe Centre and the Australian Museum, working alongside the Dharug Custodian Aboriginal Corporation. The team used drones equipped with LiDAR sensors to scan sections of the Blue Mountains, where steep terrain and dense vegetation can make traditional archaeological surveys difficult, expensive and time-consuming.LiDAR stands for Light Detection and Ranging. The technology sends laser pulses towards the ground and measures their return to build detailed three-dimensional maps of the landscape. Researchers analyse these maps to identify landforms and potential rock shelters, which are then checked through field surveys.The aerial survey identified potential locations, which researchers then visited to verify the findings. The fieldwork was led by project co-director Dr Amy Mosig Way, a research archaeologist at the University of Sydney and the Australian Museum. Students and volunteers helped assess the shelters for cultural material, while rock art recording was led by Wayne Brennan and Erin Wilkins of the Dharug Custodian Aboriginal Corporation.What the researchers found in the Blue MountainsThe field surveys confirmed the locations of six registered rock shelters and identified three previously unregistered shelters containing rock art and stone artefacts. Among the most notable discoveries were red hand stencils, traces of Aboriginal artistic expression preserved on rock surfaces. The findings also addressed a separate problem with existing heritage records. The researchers obtained more accurate geographical coordinates for known shelters than those recorded in New South Wales' Aboriginal Heritage Information Management System (AHIMS), the state's official register of Aboriginal cultural heritage sites.According to the University of Sydney, more than 200 rock shelters containing cultural and archaeological evidence have been recorded across the Blue Mountains. However, Dr Way estimates that only around 10% of the region has been surveyed because its rugged terrain makes systematic exploration challenging. The new approach could help researchers identify additional sites in areas that have received limited archaeological attention.Why the discovery matters for Aboriginal heritageThe research is part of the Gulamada Project, which brings scientific research together with First Nations cultural knowledge. Its guiding principle is to work side by side with Aboriginal communities to better understand and care for Country, a term that encompasses connections to ancestral lands, waters, culture and community. This collaboration is central to the project. The technology helps identify possible locations, but researchers still need to visit sites, verify the evidence and record cultural material with the involvement of Aboriginal custodians. The process combines aerial mapping with archaeological investigation and community knowledge.The project received $248,610 through Round 1 of the Australian Government's First Nations Heritage Grants program, administered by the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water. The program supports on-Country projects led by First Nations people to identify, document and protect heritage in existing World and National Heritage-listed places.Could drone LiDAR help uncover more sites?The study's findings suggest that drone-based LiDAR could make heritage surveys more targeted and efficient, particularly in landscapes where reaching every potential site on foot would be difficult. It could also help improve the accuracy of existing archaeological records, giving heritage managers better information about where sites are located. The researchers believe the approach could eventually be adapted to other parts of Australia. Planned future work includes testing the method in the tropical savannahs of western Arnhem Land and the semi-arid landscapes of western New South Wales.Finding and recording previously undocumented shelters could also help communities protect them from threats such as development, erosion and bushfires. The discovery does not mean that all hidden sites can be found using drones alone, but it demonstrates how remote sensing can complement ground surveys and traditional knowledge.By identifying three previously unregistered shelters, the project demonstrates how remote sensing can complement ground surveys and Aboriginal cultural knowledge, helping expand the archaeological record and support the protection of cultural landscapes for future generations.
