articles.title: Origem dos animais pode ser até 200 milhões de anos mais antiga | G1
articles.standfirst: Cientistas propõem que reino animal pode ter surgido no período Neoproterozoico, entre 800 milhões e 700 milhões de anos atrás — antes, portanto, de o planeta atravessar suas glaciações mais severas.
articles.summary: Cientistas propõem que reino animal pode ter surgido no período Neoproterozoico, entre 800 milhões e 700 milhões de anos atrás — antes, portanto, de o planeta atravessar suas glaciações mais severas.
articles.body:
Ilustração artística do fundo marinho do período Ediacarano na Namíbia, há 543 milhões de anos — Foto: Museum of Natural History, University of Oxford/Mighty Fossils

É um dos grandes enigmas da biologia evolutiva: os animais irrompem de forma relativamente repentina no registro fóssil pouco antes do período Cambriano, há entre 539 milhões e 487 milhões de anos, embora algumas evidências sugiram que sua linhagem tenha começado muito antes.

Mas, após analisar organismos microscópicos encontrados em depósitos antigos da Mongólia, uma equipe científica propôs que o reino animal possa ter surgido até 200 milhões de anos antes do que se estimava, durante o período Neoproterozoico, há entre 800 milhões e 700 milhões de anos. Antes, portanto, de o planeta atravessar suas glaciações mais severas. A conclusão consta de um estudo publicado na revista Science Advances.

A biota de Weng'an, um sítio fossilífero com cerca de 590 milhões de anos encontrado em rochas do período Ediacarano, na China, tem sido há décadas uma das principais referências para a investigação da origem da vida multicelular complexa.

Esse sítio preserva organismos microscópicos com um nível extraordinário de detalhe, mas nenhum deles pode ser considerado um animal.

Por causa dessa excepcional preservação, a comunidade científica supunha que os primeiros animais teriam surgido depois de Weng'an. A lógica era que, caso já existissem antes, um depósito de qualidade tão elevada necessariamente teria registrado seus fósseis.

Descobertas na biota de Kheseen questionam tese

O novo estudo coloca essa premissa em dúvida após analisar mais de uma centena de amostras da biota de Kheseen, na Mongólia, um conjunto de fósseis cerca de 40 milhões de anos mais jovem que Weng'an.

Na biota de Kheseen tampouco foram encontrados fósseis de animais, apesar de registros fósseis no sul da China e na Namíbia confirmarem que já havia animais na Terra naquele período.

"A biota de Kheseen refuta o argumento de que os excepcionais microfósseis de Weng'an implicam que teríamos encontrado fósseis de animais naquele depósito caso eles existissem na época", afirmou o autor Ross Anderson.

A ausência de animais num sítio de preservação excepcional não permite concluir que eles não existiam, pois podem ter vivido em ambientes diferentes dos de Kheseen, cujas condições químicas impediram sua fossilização.

"Os microfósseis de Kheseen estão igualmente bem preservados, mas ainda assim não aparecem fósseis de animais, apesar de sabermos que eles existiam naquele momento", acrescentou Anderson.

Técnica do relógio molecular apoia a hipótese

Ao rejeitar Weng'an como limite máximo para a origem dos animais, os cientistas recorreram a depósitos fossilíferos muito mais antigos, datados de 850 milhões a 730 milhões de anos, localizados na Noruega, na Austrália e no Arizona, nos Estados Unidos.

Embora esses locais também não contenham fósseis de animais, a composição química das rochas indica que elas teriam sido capazes de preservá-los caso estivessem presentes.

Com essas novas referências temporais, os pesquisadores aplicaram a técnica conhecida como relógio molecular, que analisa diferenças genéticas entre espécies atuais e as combina com a idade dos fósseis para estimar quando viveram seus ancestrais comuns.

O resultado foi um recuo de cerca de 200 milhões de anos na estimativa para a origem do reino animal, situando-a entre 800 milhões e 700 milhões de anos atrás, muito antes dos primeiros fósseis corporais confirmados.

Glaciações globais do período Criogeniano

A hipótese coincide com a presença de biomarcadores químicos em rochas antigas, interpretados como possíveis evidências de esponjas primitivas que viveram há pelo menos 650 milhões de anos.

Tratava-se de organismos minúsculos, de corpo mole e com baixíssima probabilidade de fossilização quando comparados à fauna posterior, que passou a apresentar conchas, ossos ou outras estruturas resistentes.

Além disso, situar a origem dos animais entre 800 milhões e 700 milhões de anos atrás implica que os estágios iniciais de sua evolução coincidiram com as glaciações globais do período Criogeniano, iniciadas há cerca de 720 milhões de anos, quando grande parte do planeta estava coberta por gelo, num fenômeno conhecido como "Terra Bola de Neve".

Os resultados ajudam a esclarecer "o que sabemos sobre os ritmos da evolução, o momento em que surgem as inovações biológicas e os processos que levam à diversificação dos animais", afirmou o coautor Derek Briggs, professor da Universidade Yale.

No entanto, os cientistas ressaltam que o estudo não demonstra de forma definitiva a existência de animais há 800 milhões de anos. O trabalho mostra apenas que a ausência de fósseis de animais num sítio específico não é suficiente para descartar essa possibilidade, abrindo espaço para que análises moleculares revelem uma história evolutiva muito mais antiga.

"Até que a evidência esteja disponível, a data exata de surgimento do reino animal continua incerta", conclui Anderson.

articles.title: Neandertal pode ter sido morto por lança há 75 mil anos | G1
articles.standfirst: Ferimento na escápula indica que golpe com lança teria vindo de frente. Pesquisadores não descartam acidente de caça, mas dizem que padrão é compatível com ataque de perto.
articles.summary: Ferimento na escápula sugere golpe dado de frente e pode ser rara evidência de violência no Paleolítico. Acidente de caça ainda não foi descartado.
articles.body:
Escápula esquerda de Shanidar A, fóssil de neandertal que viveu há cerca de 75 mil anos, analisada por pesquisadores da Universidade de Cambridge. — Foto: University of Cambridge

Um neandertal que viveu há cerca de 75 mil anos pode ter sido morto por uma lança de madeira usada a um curta distância. Pelo menos, é isso o que aponta um novo estudo publicado na revista "Scientific Reports".

A análise de um ferimento no ombro indica que a arma pode ter sido usada a curta distância e traz uma rara evidência de violência no Paleolítico.

Os restos pertencem a um indivíduo chamado pelos pesquisadores de Shanidar A, encontrado na caverna de Shanidar, no Curdistão iraquiano.

Ele tinha cerca de 45 anos, uma idade avançada para os padrões neandertais, e seus restos incluem parte da mão direita, costelas, dentes e a escápula esquerda.

Foi justamente na escápula que os arqueólogos encontraram a principal pista: um buraco quase perfeitamente circular, de cerca de 15 milímetros de diâmetro, cercado por pequenas fraturas. Fragmentos do próprio osso ainda estavam preservados logo abaixo da perfuração.

A equipe descartou explicações como raízes de plantas, ação de insetos ou danos provocados durante a escavação.

Exames microscópicos e imagens de microtomografia também não mostraram sinais de cicatrização, o que indica que o ferimento ocorreu muito perto do momento da morte.

Ainda segundo o estudo, o formato da perfuração é uma das razões para a hipótese da lança. Pontas de pedra costumam deixar marcas mais angulares, enquanto armas de madeira produzem perfurações arredondadas.

Lanças de madeira preservadas em sítios muito mais antigos da Europa têm dimensões compatíveis com o buraco encontrado na escápula.

A trajetória do ferimento também chamou a atenção dos pesquisadores. A arma teria entrado pela frente do corpo, atravessado tecidos e órgãos do tórax antes de atingir a escápula. Segundo a equipe, o golpe poderia ter atingido o pulmão e grandes vasos sanguíneos, provocando uma morte rápida.

“Nunca podemos ter certeza, porque a madeira não se preservou, mas uma lança de madeira parece a explicação mais provável”, disse ao g1 Emma Pomeroy, arqueóloga da Universidade de Cambridge e principal autora do estudo.

Não é possível afirmar que Shanidar A tenha sido assassinado. Um acidente durante uma caçada continua sendo uma explicação possível.

Mas a análise do osso trouxe um detalhe que reforça a hipótese de confronto: a fratura parece mais compatível com uma lança usada para golpear de perto do que com uma arma arremessada à distância.

“Com uma lança de estocada, é preciso estar muito perto de alguém quando se ataca. E sabemos que o ferimento veio pela frente, então Shanidar A provavelmente estava de frente para quem o atingiu”, explicou Pomeroy ao g1.

A pesquisadora ressalta que ainda são necessários mais testes experimentais para reconstruir exatamente o que aconteceu. Também não há como saber se, caso tenha ocorrido um ataque, ele partiu de alguém do mesmo grupo ou de outro.

Registros desse tipo são raros. A maior parte das evidências conhecidas de violência organizada na Pré-História é muito mais recente, associada a sociedades agrícolas.

Por isso, um possível ataque fatal entre indivíduos no Paleolítico ajuda a ampliar o que se sabe sobre conflitos entre populações humanas antigas.

Entrada da caverna de Shanidar, no Curdistão iraquiano, sítio arqueológico conhecido pela descoberta de restos de neandertais. — Foto: Graeme Barker

Os restos de Shanidar A também contam uma história diferente. Um dos incisivos havia sido partido longitudinalmente após um trauma grave no rosto, mas continuou sendo usado por bastante tempo depois da lesão. O desgaste e o acúmulo de tártaro indicam que ele sobreviveu ao ferimento.

Pomeroy afirma que o indivíduo provavelmente teve dificuldades para comer, beber e se comunicar durante a recuperação e pode ter recebido ajuda de outros integrantes do grupo.

Ela pondera, porém, que não é possível medir quanto dessa sobrevivência dependeu de cuidados e quanto resultou da própria capacidade de adaptação.

Para a arqueóloga, é justamente essa combinação que torna o caso especialmente interessante.

“Vemos duas facetas contrastantes da natureza humana, o cuidado e a violência, reunidas no mesmo indivíduo".

Shanidar A também foi depositado em um ponto específico da caverna, atrás de uma grande rocha. Nos anos ou décadas seguintes, pelo menos outros quatro neandertais foram colocados praticamente no mesmo local, em diferentes momentos.

A repetição reforça a interpretação de que aquele espaço tinha algum significado para o grupo. Segundo os pesquisadores, o conjunto acrescenta evidências de que os neandertais não apenas cuidavam de indivíduos feridos, mas também mantinham práticas deliberadas relacionadas aos mortos.

Incisivo de Shanidar A partido ao meio após um trauma sofrido em vida. O desgaste indica que o neandertal sobreviveu ao ferimento. — Foto: Emma Pomeroy

articles.title: Starlink: Elon Musk pode desligar a internet de uma guerra? Entenda | G1
articles.standfirst: Criada para levar conexão a regiões remotas, rede de satélites virou ferramenta essencial em conflitos e protestos, da Ucrânia ao Irã. Dependência da tecnologia de Musk preocupa governos e acelera a busca por alternativas.
articles.summary: Criada para levar conexão a regiões remotas, rede de satélites virou ferramenta essencial em conflitos e protestos, da Ucrânia ao Irã.
articles.body:
Seja nos desertos inóspitos do Saara ou na densa Floresta Amazônica, na imensidão do Oceano Pacífico ou na camada de gelo do Ártico, em muitas partes do mundo não existe acesso à internet.

Originalmente, o bilionário sul-africano da tecnologia Elon Musk promoveu o desenvolvimento da Starlink para resolver precisamente esse problema, levando internet de alta velocidade a regiões do mundo onde cabos ou fibra ótica não chegam; ou onde isso é tão caro que simplesmente não compensa.

Entretanto, a gama de aplicações da Starlink expandiu-se consideravelmente. O sistema passou a ser utilizado para comunicação em áreas de desastre e também por exércitos ou movimentos de protesto – por exemplo, em áreas onde a internet original foi destruída por fogo inimigo ou bloqueada por regimes ditatoriais.

Rede Starlink tem quase 10 mil pequenos satélites em órbita baixa — Foto: La Nacion/ZUMA Press/picture alliance

Essencialmente, trata-se de um sistema de internet via satélite com quase 10 mil pequenos satélites orbitando a Terra.

Eles retransmitem pacotes de dados entre si por meio de feixes de laser e não exigem uma linha de visão direta e constante com uma estação terrestre que conecte o sistema de satélites à internet convencional.

Ao contrário de outros satélites de internet, que orbitam a uma altitude de aproximadamente 36 mil quilômetros, os satélites Starlink estão localizados a apenas cerca de 550 quilômetros acima da superfície da Terra .

Isso permite que os sinais de internet sejam transmitidos muito mais rapidamente. A latência é mantida tão baixa que permite o funcionamento até mesmo de aplicações que exigem grande quantidade de dados.

Os usuários precisam apenas de um pequeno terminal receptor com uma antena controlada eletronicamente que se alinha automaticamente com os satélites que passam.

Esses terminais, então, encaminham o sinal recebido para um roteador próximo, que fornece a conexão de internet dentro da rede local.

Musk promoveu o desenvolvimento da Starlink para prover internet a zonas remotas — Foto: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Ucrânia: Desde o início da guerra de agressão da Rússia, em fevereiro de 2022, a Starlink tornou-se uma das ferramentas de comunicação mais importantes na zona de guerra .

Os militares utilizam o Starlink para coordenar unidades, operar drones e controlar sistemas terrestres não tripulados.

No setor civil, o sistema é utilizado por hospitais, serviços de emergência, fornecedores de energia e a ferrovia ucraniana, entre outros.

Alega-se também que o Exército russo está acessando a Starlink usando terminais contrabandeados ilegalmente para o país através de países intermediários.

O Ministério da Defesa da Ucrânia afirmou que trabalha em estreita colaboração com a operadora, SpaceX, para restringir ao máximo esse uso.

Sudão: Na guerra civil sudanesa, a Starlink é usada principalmente pelas Forças de Apoio Rápido (RSF), grupo paramilitar que luta contra o Exército estatal.

Centenas de dispositivos foram contrabandeados para o país através dos Emirados Árabes Unidos, e um verdadeiro mercado negro de terminais Starlink se estabeleceu.

As RSF usam esses dispositivos para comunicação e coordenação entre suas milícias, enquanto as Forças Armadas Sudanesas (SAF) tentam bloquear sua importação e uso.

Irã: No início deste ano, protestos em todo o país eclodiram contra o regime em Teerã, que respondeu, entre outras coisas, desligando a internet. No entanto, relatos indicam que milhares de terminais foram contrabandeados para o país e revendidos no mercado ilegal.

Isso permitiu que manifestantes usassem a Starlink para coordenar seus atos contra o regime, apesar da censura estatal da internet.

Venezuela: A Starlink também já foi usada no passado para burlar restrições de informação e garantir acesso gratuito à internet. Durante muito tempo, o serviço só esteve disponível extraoficialmente, através da compra de kits no comércio local.

Após a intervenção dos EUA e a captura de Nicolás Maduro, Elon Musk ofereceu temporariamente acesso gratuito à internet aos cidadãos do país.

Usuário precisa só de um terminal receptor com antena, que encaminha o sinal a um roteador próximo — Foto: Middle East Images/picture alliance

Faixa de Gaza: Desde julho de 2024, a Starlink tem sido usada para fins humanitários em uma Faixa de Gaza amplamente destruída.

Organizações de ajuda humanitária e um hospital de campanha podem utilizá-lo para fornecer assistência por telemedicina e coordenação logística.

No entanto, o acesso generalizado para civis permanece limitado, em parte devido a preocupações de segurança por parte de Israel.

A Starlink costuma ser a única conexão de internet em zonas de conflito. Isso confere a Elon Musk uma enorme influência. Em alguns casos, a comunicação de forças armadas inteiras ou organizações humanitárias depende de sua empresa, a SpaceX.

Por exemplo, Musk já se recusou a ativar o serviço para a Ucrânia durante um ataque perto da Crimeia.

O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, também ameaçou a Ucrânia com o desligamento dos satélites para forçar Kiev a fazer concessões nas negociações.

Há também críticas do ponto de vista ecológico. Os satélites Starlink são produzidos em massa e têm uma vida útil de apenas cerca de cinco anos.

Em média, um ou dois satélites de Musk se desintegram na atmosfera terrestre todos os dias; o óxido de alumínio liberado nesse processo pode afetar a camada de ozônio e contribuir para o aquecimento global.

Além disso, os numerosos satélites refletem a luz solar, tornando o céu noturno mais claro, o que também pode ter um impacto sobre a vida selvagem.

Ferramenta vital em conflitos: soldado ucraniano com receptor de Starlink — Foto: Alexander Polegenko/picture alliance

Apesar de todas as preocupações, alternativas já estão sendo desenvolvidas, principalmente na Europa, para quebrar o monopólio da Starlink.

O maior concorrente privado da SpaceX atualmente é a Eutelsat. No entanto, seu serviço de satélite, OneWeb, com uma frota de mais de 600 satélites, é significativamente menor. Além disso, o serviço se concentra em clientes corporativos e aplicações marítimas.

A Eutelsat também está envolvida no desenvolvimento da IRIS², uma ambiciosa rede de satélites de alta segurança da União Europeia.

Essa rede visa tornar a Europa menos dependente da Starlink. Contudo, ela não estará operacional antes de 2029.

Elon Musk também enfrenta concorrência nos EUA, principalmente de seu colega bilionário Jeff Bezos . A empresa de Bezos, a Amazon, está trabalhando intensamente em seu serviço Amazon Leo: a construção de uma rede com mais de 3 mil novos satélites em órbita baixa da Terra.

A Amazon planeja estrear seu serviço comercialmente ainda neste ano – inclusive no Brasil, graças a uma parceria com a Sky.

Os céus estão prestes a ficar mais congestionados , especialmente porque a China está desenvolvendo dois sistemas próprios de comunicação via satélite.

O projeto estatal Guowang é voltado principalmente para uso nacional e militar e prevê a inclusão de até 13 mil satélites, enquanto o projeto Qianfan, com aproximadamente 12 mil satélites, tem uma orientação mais comercial e destina-se a atender países emergentes e em desenvolvimento.

Os primeiros lançamentos em massa para ambos os projetos também estão programados para este ano.

articles.title: Made in India isn’t enough. It has to be made by India
articles.summary: India needs to change its slogan. Across critical sectors, the ambition must move from Made in India to Made by India.
articles.body: India needs to change its slogan. Across critical sectors, the ambition must move from Made in India to Made by India.The distinction may sound like a play on words, but it goes to the heart of what it means to become a technological power. Made in India tells us where a product was manufactured. Made by India tells us who invented it, who owns the intellectual property (IP), who controls the technology and who captures the value it creates.This isn’t an attempt to deny the importance of manufacturing. Factories create jobs, build industrial capabilities, enable supplier networks and reduce dependence on imported finished products. Assembling mobile phones at scale, developing the capacity to launch satellites or manufacturing sophisticated equipment are all milestones.But India must stop treating every new assembly line, every imported technology given a domestic label and every payload bought from elsewhere as evidence of having arrived, lest it wants to become a country that manufactures the future without owning it.Take smartphones, for example. India has made progress in becoming a manufacturing and export base for mobile phones. Yet in Aug 2026, MeitY secretary S Krishnan said domestic value addition in mobile phones is only at 22-23%. The figure shows the distance between assembling a finished product and developing the technologies and designs that go into it.The same principle applies to space. Buying a payload — like atomic clocks for instance — and operating it successfully can serve a legitimate strategic need (it’s another matter that India’s NavIC programme is dysfunctional). But acquiring technology is not the same as creating it. That experience must build the capacity to design, develop and improve technology independently.IP is not merely a legal certificate or a patent number. It’s an economic asset, and in strategic sectors, a source of leverage that determines who licenses technology, earns royalties and develops the next generation of a product.India needs both manufacturing muscle and intellectual ownership and it cannot afford to confuse the former with the latter.The semiconductor industry makes for a good case. India has a large pool of chip-design engineers, and the govt has recognised that talent through initiatives such as the Design Linked Incentive (DLI) scheme, which supports domestic companies and startups working on semiconductor design and IP.The goal should be to turn these capabilities into globally competitive designs, products and sustainable businesses. This won’t happen overnight. That’s precisely why the country needs a long-term strategy rather than a succession of announcements measured by investment commitments, factories inaugurated or projects launched.The broader research picture makes the case more pressing. India's gross expenditure on R&D stood at about 0.8% of GDP in 2023-24, according to govt figures. India has a substantial scientific and engineering workforce, but its ability to translate research into internationally competitive products remains a critical challenge.India lacks an ecosystem that takes an idea from a lab to a patent, from a patent to a working prototype, and from a prototype to a product customers will buy. A patent by itself is not proof of commercial success.This is not an argument against foreign investment, collaboration or imported technology. It’s an argument against permanent dependence in strategic sectors. Partnerships should expand India's capabilities, not leave essential design and ownership beyond its control.Nor should indigenous IP become an excuse for protectionism. Buying technology can be the right decision. So can licensing it or working with a foreign partner. The question is whether these choices help develop domestic capabilities or become a substitute for doing so.The govt must measure progress differently. Alongside factories, production volumes and exports, it should track Indian-owned technologies, commercialised research, licensing revenues and original products reaching global markets.Companies must invest in research, universities must strengthen industry links, and investors must recognise that deep technology often requires longer timelines.The public conversation needs to change, too. There’s nothing wrong with celebrating a factory opening or a successful mission. But celebrations should reflect the achievement, not inflate it into proof that the larger challenge has been overcome. When standards are set too low, incremental progress can be mistaken for the destination. The result is stagnation disguised as success.India's ambition must be higher. It must aim not only to make products the world buys, but also to create the technologies the world needs. Building IP takes time. It demands patience, investment and a willingness to accept failure. It also requires resisting the temptation to declare victory at every intermediate milestone.India must learn to look at technological progress like a marathon runner, not a PR agency!The Parallax is simple: a product may be made in India without its technology being made by India. The real test is whether, when the next generation arrives, India can build it on its own terms.

articles.title: Astronomers discover green star 280 light-years away; what makes it glow green
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered a star that appears green, an unusual celestial sight that could change how scientists understand the colours of dying stars.
articles.body: Astronomers have discovered a star that appears green, an unusual celestial sight that could change how scientists understand the colours of dying stars.According to a study published in RAS Techniques and Instruments, the white dwarf WD J1330+6435 lies about 280 light-years from Earth in the constellation Draco and has a chartreuse-green hue caused by the way sodium interacts with helium under the star’s intense atmospheric conditions.The discovery is part of a broader study into the unusual colours of white dwarfs, the dense remnants left behind when stars exhaust their nuclear fuel and shed their outer layers.According to CNN, the researchers found that the chemical composition of a white dwarf’s atmosphere can significantly alter the light it emits, making some of these stellar remnants appear in colours beyond those typically associated with stars.“The colors that normal stars can have are pretty much only orange, white or blue,” Mark Hollands, an astrophysicist at the University of Warwick in England and lead author of the study, told CNN.He explained that the unusual green appearance of WD J1330+6435 is linked to the physical conditions in its atmosphere, which alter the wavelengths of light absorbed by the star.The green appearance of WD J1330+6435 is linked to the behaviour of sodium in the white dwarf’s extremely dense atmosphere.Under these conditions, sodium interacts with helium in ways that alter the wavelengths of light absorbed by the star, while other elements, including calcium, also influence its spectrum. Researchers used spectral data and models of human colour perception to calculate how the star would appear, rather than relying on a direct photograph showing it as green, according to CNN.The green star 280 light-years awayThe green star, WD J1330+6435, is located about 280 light-years from Earth in the constellation Draco. But what does that distance actually mean?A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, around 9.46 trillion kilometres. So, the light travelling from this star takes approximately 280 years to reach Earth. When astronomers observe it today, they are effectively looking at the star as it appeared 280 years ago.The white dwarf has an estimated temperature of around 4,000 degrees Celsius and is extremely compact, roughly comparable in size to Earth.

articles.title: Rubio says Ukraine without access to Starshield, future ‘under discussion’
articles.summary: Top US diplomat says Ukraine has requested access to military-grade version of Starlink for strikes deep inside Russia.
articles.body:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Starshield , the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite service, is currently unavailable to Ukraine, but a request from Kyiv to access the system for attacks deep inside Russia is “under discussion”.

Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Rubio stressed Starshield’s distinction with Starlink, the internet service provided by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

“Starlink is a commercial product, okay? And so it’s regulated and handled as a commercial product. Starshield is a defence product, a military product,” said Rubio, in comments released by the Department of State.

“They’ve asked for access to it in order to conduct deep strikes inside of Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment,” he added. “That’s under conversation.”

Launched in 2022 and provided to the US government, Starshield is designed for military use as it allows for deeper encryption to process sensitive information. SpaceX says it is primarily used by US defence agencies and other “government partners”.

Last week, Ukrainian officials said restrictions on Starlink terminals had slowed some drones on the battlefield, as Ukraine tries to hold back Russian forces in their nearly five-year war.

In his comments at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, Rubio also rejected Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s suggestion that the reported disruption to Starlink services in Ukraine on Wednesday was deliberate.

“Well, I don’t know what Zelenskyy said. I’m not sure Zelenskyy knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate. We have nothing to do with that,” Rubio said.

Zelenskyy said on Saturday that the satellites are not tracking antennas on flying objects travelling faster than 161 kilometres per hour (100 miles per hour). This is affecting Ukrainian drones in their defence against Russian jet-powered drones and in their own medium-range attacks, he added.

Rubio said the US had not ordered Starlink speeds to be reduced and that the service had reportedly been restored to its previous level.

“No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it,” he said, calling the reports “categorically false”.

The remarks came as US President Donald Trump drew criticism from Democrats and Republicans after waiving sanctions on Russia and countries that buy its oil and gas, days before the restrictions were due to take effect under a law he signed last month.

Zelenskyy also criticised the sanctions waiver on Saturday, saying easing pressure on Russia would encourage further attacks.

“Financial rewards for [President Vladimir] Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” Zelenskyy posted on social media, urging the US to maintain pressure on Moscow.

articles.title: Nasa grew crystals from a protein found in human tears aboard ISS; scientists use them to study how proteins form in space
articles.summary: Nasa has grown crystals of lysozyme, a protein found in human tears, saliva and milk, aboard the International Space Station (ISS) to study how crystals
articles.body: Nasa has grown crystals of lysozyme, a protein found in human tears, saliva and milk, aboard the International Space Station (ISS) to study how crystals form in microgravity. The experiment offers a closer look at how proteins develop under conditions that differ from those on Earth. According to Nasa, the crystals were produced using Redwire’s PIL-BOX hardware as part of research into crystal formation in space. Although lysozyme is a familiar biological substance, studying its crystals can help researchers understand the processes involved in producing high-quality crystals for scientific investigations.How Nasa grew crystals from a protein found in human tearsNasa shared an image of lysozyme crystals aboard the International Space Station, taken on June 5, 2024. In its report, the agency explained that lysozyme is present in bodily fluids, including tears, saliva and milk, and plays an important role in the body’s natural defences against harmful microorganisms.The protein helps protect the body against bacteria, viruses and fungi, making it an important component of the innate immune system. Researchers also use lysozyme as a control compound to demonstrate the formation of well-shaped crystals.The crystals were grown using Redwire’s PIL-BOX, a piece of experimental hardware used to investigate how microgravity affects crystal production. The work forms part of a broader effort to understand how crystals develop in the unusual environment of space.Why proteins are studied in crystalline formProteins perform a wide range of functions in the human body, from supporting the immune system to regulating essential biological processes. Their shapes are closely linked to how they work, and even small differences in structure can influence their behaviour.Nasa explained that understanding protein structures can help researchers develop medicines that interact with specific targets in the body.Many treatments work by binding to a particular protein and changing its activity. To design medicines that interact with these targets effectively, scientists need detailed information about their 3D structures.Growing proteins into crystals provides one way to obtain that information. Researchers can examine the crystals using techniques such as X-ray diffraction, which reveals details about the arrangement of atoms within a protein.However, obtaining crystals suitable for detailed analysis can be difficult. Their quality affects how accurately scientists can determine a protein’s structure, making the conditions under which they grow an important part of the research.Microgravity changes the way crystals developOn Earth, gravity influences the movement of liquids and particles during crystal formation. Processes such as sedimentation, in which heavier particles settle, and convection, which causes fluids to move because of temperature or density differences, can interfere with the growth of an orderly crystal.The ISS offers a different environment. In microgravity, these gravity-driven effects are reduced, allowing protein molecules to come together and arrange themselves within a crystal more gradually.The ISS National Laboratory explained this process which examined research using the station to grow medically important molecular crystals. They noted that proteins grown in microgravity can form larger, more orderly crystals than those produced under comparable conditions on Earth.The ESA has also described in its report on the high-quality protein crystal growth experiment in the Kibo laboratory, how reduced convection and the absence of ordinary gravitational settling can help proteins form crystals with fewer structural imperfections.Importance of this research for medical scienceThe study of lysozyme crystals fits into a wider programme of research exploring how microgravity can improve scientists’ understanding of proteins. Although lysozyme serves as a control compound in the experiment described by Nasa, other protein crystallisation investigations have more direct connections medical applications.According to the ISS National Laboratory, researchers have used the station to investigate proteins associated with conditions such as heart disease, liver disease and cancer. Understanding the structures of these proteins can provide information that may eventually support the development of treatments.Nasa described research involving Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a genetic disorder that affects muscles. A Japanese research team used information about the structure of a protein associated with the disease to identify potential compounds for treatment. One candidate, TAS-205, subsequently underwent clinical investigation.Space-based experiments support research on EarthProtein crystallisation experiments have been conducted aboard the ISS for decades. Researchers from pharmaceutical companies and academic institutions had carried out more than 500 protein crystal growth experiments on the station by 2021.Research has also explored whether improved crystallisation techniques could help pharmaceutical companies develop more stable drug formulations or medicines that are easier to administer. Nasa described investigations into monoclonal antibodies, for example, that examined ways to improve the consistency of formulations used in cancer treatment.The broader aim is to improve scientific understanding of proteins and support research that could eventually contribute to better medicines and treatments.

articles.title: Four University of Washington students built a wallet-sized patch that gives rescuers real-time LED guidance during CPR; the invention has now won the 2026 Collegiate Inventors Competition and a $10,000 prize
articles.summary: Performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) during an emergency can be difficult for someone without proper training.
articles.body: Performing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) during an emergency can be difficult for someone without proper training. Even when a bystander is willing to help, getting the depth and speed of chest compressions right can be challenging. Four University of Washington students have developed a wallet-sized device that provides visual guidance during CPR. Their invention, called CPRight, won the $10,000 undergraduate first prize at the 2026 Collegiate Inventors Competition, announced on Friday.According to National Inventors Hall of Fame's (NIHF), the device is a small, single-use patch that uses LED lights to indicate whether chest compressions are being performed effectively. Unlike systems that depend on external equipment, CPRight works independently, allowing rescuers to receive feedback while performing CPR.Shubham Bansal, Prisha Hemani, Deeya Sharma and Nikhita Vaddineni developed the invention under the guidance of Tristan Jafari. Their work was recognised at a national competition organised by the National Inventors Hall of Fame (NIHF), which rewards inventions created by university students.The invention addresses a serious problem in emergency medical care. According to the NIHF, more than 350,000 Americans experience out-of-hospital cardiac emergencies annually, with approximately 90% dying. The figures cited by the organisation highlight the importance of effective emergency assistance, particularly when medical professionals are not immediately available.How the patch helps someone performing CPRThe idea behind CPRight is to give rescuers immediate information about their chest compressions without requiring them to operate another device.Before starting compressions, the rescuer places the patch on the patient's sternum, commonly known as the breastbone. As CPR is performed, its LED indicators show whether the depth and rate of compressions are effective.The patch does not need to be connected to a smartphone or monitoring system. This allows the person performing CPR to receive visual guidance directly from the device.The students have also kept the design compact. Its wallet-sized form and single-use design are intended to make it a practical option for emergency situations.CPRight was one of several medical inventions recognised at this year's competition. While the University of Washington team focused on emergency resuscitation, other student groups worked on problems involving cancer treatment, rehabilitation, shoulder injuries and neurological monitoring.From knee recovery to monitoring brain activityOne of the other recognised inventions aims to help people recovering from knee injuries or surgery. Rehabilitation can continue for months, and patients may need to perform exercises at home between appointments.Students at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill developed KAIRS, short for Knee Artificial Intelligence Rehabilitation Sleeve, to track movement during this recovery period.The system uses sensors embedded in a flexible sleeve to measure knee movement and range of motion. Information collected by the sleeve is processed through a mobile application and a cloud-based machine learning model.This allows patients to follow their progress while clinicians can review their movements remotely. The invention could also help people who have difficulty accessing regular physical therapy.The team of Samanyu Dixit, Hieu Minh Doan, Sahaj Sapovadia and Chinmay Singh, advised by Devin Hubbard, received the $5,000 undergraduate runner-up award.Another team focused on making brain monitoring more comfortable. Researchers at the University of South Florida developed NeuTrode, a flexible electrode for electroencephalography (EEG), which records electrical activity in the brain.EEG is used to investigate conditions such as epilepsy, sleep disorders and brain injuries. NeuTrode is designed to maintain contact with the scalp without gels or liquids, while accommodating different hair densities, skin conditions and head shapes.Developed by Bridget Clift, Cristina Ramirez-Vargas and Addison Whitehead under adviser Nathan Schilaty, the invention received the $2,000 People's Choice Award.Inventions focus on cancer treatment and shoulder repairThe competition also recognised a device intended to address difficulties faced by patients undergoing radiation treatment after jaw reconstruction.Patients with head and neck cancer sometimes require jaw reconstruction following tumour removal. Titanium plates used to secure the reconstructed jaw can interfere with subsequent radiation treatment.These plates may prevent radiation from reaching some tumour cells while scattering it towards healing tissue. According to the NIHF, approximately 60% of patients develop a complication within five years.To address this, a University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine team developed ClearView-Jaw, which is designed to reduce radiation backscatter and shadowing. The invention aims to help clinicians direct radiation more precisely.William McKay, Zachary Spears and Amogh Vellore, advised by Anish Ghodadra and Matthew Spector, received the $10,000 graduate first prize.The graduate runner-up award went to BioAxis, a device associated with New York University and developed by Vitalis Regenerative Materials Inc.BioAxis is intended for partial-thickness rotator cuff tears, which affect approximately three million Americans annually. It combines a patient's platelet-rich plasma with a bioresorbable polymer to form a hydrogel that adheres to tissue, supporting tendon preservation and repair. The team of Rayan Bargouth and Asser El Ashwah, advised by Richard Stein, received $5,000.Collegiate Inventors CompetitionEstablished in 1990, the Collegiate Inventors Competition is organised by the NIHF and sponsored by the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO).This year's competition brought together 25 students from nine US colleges and universities. Ten finalist teams presented their inventions to judges drawn from the NIHF and USPTO. Along with their cash awards, winning teams receive a USPTO Patent Acceleration Certificate.The competition has recognised more than 500 innovators since its establishment, supporting student inventions with potential for patent protection.

articles.title: A Labrador once trained for mountain rescue becomes a marine conservation detection dog; Sgiath can sniff out the invasive organism known as “sea vomit” and wins IFAW's 2026 Animal of the Year Award
articles.summary: A six-year-old black Labrador from the Scottish Highlands in the UK has found an unusual new role in conservation.
articles.body: A six-year-old black Labrador from the Scottish Highlands in the UK has found an unusual new role in conservation. Sgiath, who was originally trained as a mountain rescue search dog, can now detect an invasive marine organism known as “sea vomit” by smell. Her work has earned her the 2026 Animal of the Year Award from the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW). According to IFAW’s announcement, Sgiath is believed to be the first dog in the world trained to detect ‘Didemnum vexillum,’ commonly called carpet sea squirt or “sea vomit”. She works alongside her handler, marine ecologist Dr Texa Sim, to help locate the organism in UK waters.Sgiath received the award at IFAW’s annual Animal Action Awards ceremony, held at BAFTA in London on October 15. The event recognised six people and one animal for their contributions to conservation and animal welfare.What is ‘sea vomit’ and why is it a concern?Despite its nickname, sea vomit is not vomit. It is an invasive marine organism that can grow in thick, slimy colonies on seaweed, pontoons, oyster cages and other marine structures. According to IFAW, the species can spread rapidly and poses a threat to native marine life. As reported by The Independent carpet sea squirt can spread across harbours and oyster farms, where it can smother native organisms and become difficult to control once established.The organism is believed to have originated in Japan and was first reported on shorelines in England and Wales in 2008, according to a BBC report. Its appearance can make it difficult to distinguish from other marine growth. Finding it early is important because conventional identification can require specialist laboratory analysis and DNA testing. Sgiath offers another way to search for it: using her sense of smell.How Sgiath moved from mountain rescue to marine conservationSgiath was initially trained as a mountain rescue search dog. Her ability to track scents led Sim, a marine ecologist, to explore whether the Labrador could help identify an invasive species threatening marine habitats. The idea developed while Sim was working on a native oyster restoration project on Scotland’s west coast. She recognised that dogs, already used to locate invasive plants and animals on land, might also help detect an invasive organism in the marine environment. The early results were encouraging.Sgiath has since been trained to give a passive indication when she detects the organism. Rather than barking or rushing towards it, she signals the find by becoming still and staring at the target. This is different from the more active indication she was trained to use during mountain rescue work. According to the BBC, Sgiath has already discovered hundreds of colonies of the invasive sea squirt.Why a dog’s nose could help conservationistsDetecting an invasive species before it spreads widely can give conservation teams more time to respond. Sgiath’s scent-based searches could help identify the organism in places where visual inspection alone may not be enough. Her work is also helping explore a new use for detection dogs in marine conservation. IFAW described the project as a pioneering approach to tackling invasive marine species in UK waters. The approach does not replace all existing detection methods, but it could provide conservationists and site managers with another tool for finding the species earlier and more efficiently.Another Labrador is learning the jobSgiath is not the only dog involved in the project. Sim is also training Uisge, a three-year-old Labrador, to detect the invasive organism and support the work. According to West Coast Today, the dogs have demonstrated an ability to distinguish the target species from other sea squirts and marine organisms, including detecting traces of its scent in water samples. Their work could become increasingly useful if changing sea conditions allow invasive marine species to spread into new areas. Early detection is particularly important because established colonies can be difficult and expensive to manage.

articles.title: With the Crew Dragon retiring, NASA needs a new plan for low Earth orbit
articles.summary: The matter has achieved some urgency since NASA has officially issued a request for private companies to propose their own space stations.
articles.body:
SpaceX has indicated that it would cease launches of its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets to concentrate on the Starship by the end of the International Space Station’s operation in 2030. The decision presents a problem , especially to companies planning their own commercial space stations, because it means that the Dragon spacecraft will no longer fly.

The matter has achieved some urgency since NASA has officially issued a request for private companies to propose their own space stations. According to Ars Technica, these companies likely include Axiom Space, Voyager Space and Vast Space. Blue Origin is working on its own space station but it is unclear whether it will answer the request. SpaceX is considered not likely to bid, at least for now.

To keep access to low Earth orbit available, NASA and Boeing are working to revive the trouble-prone Starliner. Starliner has had two uncrewed flights , the first being unsuccessful. Its sole crewed flight resulted in astronauts Sunita Williams and Butch Wilmore being stuck on the International Space Station because of glitches that made Starliner unsafe to return to Earth with a crew. Williams and Wilmore later returned on board a Crew Dragon.

In an agreement with NASA , Boeing will undertake a number of fixes that will presumably make Starliner flightworthy. NASA plans a cargo flight of the Starliner around December or January, and another attempt at a crewed flight in 2028.

Blue Origin is the other American company with the ability to develop a new spacecraft capable of taking people and cargo to and from low Earth orbit. It turns out that Blue Origin is working on a spacecraft, dubbed the Space Vehicle, which Ars Technica’s Eric Berger said has been making “substantial progress”.

However, before going to the next level to build flyable hardware, Blue Origin needs some buy-in from NASA similar to what Boeing is getting for Starliner. Developing a spacecraft on its own dime is a monumental challenge, even for a company backed by Jeff Bezos’ deep pockets.

NASA would be well advised to give its official seal of approval to the Blue Origin Space Vehicle, as well as some cash. The original Commercial Crew policy of funding two spacecraft turned out to be a wise decision when the Boeing Starliner fell short, but the SpaceX Crew Dragon came through , time after time.

With the planned end of Crew Dragon flights, SpaceX is conducting test flights of its Starship. When operational, the largest human-made object ever to fly in space will be a quantum leap in space launch capability. It will open up the solar system to human activity. Nothing like it is in development anywhere else.

Still, the fact of the Dragon going away has left the nascent commercial space station sector in something of a lurch, pending the advent of the Boeing Starliner and, presumably, the Blue Origin Space Vehicle.

Could the Crew Dragon and the Falcon family of launch vehicles be extended?

SpaceX is under no obligation to provide a service past the launches that it has been contracted to provide. It is a private business and free to deliver a launch service or not, depending on its business needs.

Using the Starship to send people and cargo to and from commercial space stations would seem like overkill. The spacecraft is capable of sending up to 150 metric tons of anything anywhere (with refueling) in the solar system, far and above the four or so astronauts and the cargo that a commercial space station would need.

Indeed, a Starship could be outfitted as a commercial space station and deployed in one launch. Little evidence exists that SpaceX is planning such a thing, but who knows?

One possibility would be to spin off the Dragon, the Falcon 9 and the Falcon Heavy into a separate company and then sell it to investors who would then run it to service the commercial space stations. Call it Dragon Spaceline.

SpaceX could then use the money to further enhance the Starship and related space businesses, such as Starlink and the planned space-based data centers.

Everybody wins: SpaceX, the commercial space station companies and NASA. Or rather, almost everybody since Boeing and Blue Origin would have a competitor with a proven track record of success.

NASA has vowed that it is not abandoning low Earth orbit as it shoots for the moon, Mars and beyond. Future decisions will reveal how serious that vow is.

Mark R. Whittington, who writes frequently about space policy, has published a political study of space exploration entitled “ Why is It So Hard to Go Back to the Moon? ” as well as “ The Moon, Mars and Beyond ” and, most recently, “ Why is America Going Back to the Moon? ” He blogs at Curmudgeons Corner.

articles.title: In 2023, California scientists moved 246 endangered black abalone to a protected coastline; three years later, site counts rose from 54 to 302, density hit 1 per sq metre and juveniles appeared
articles.summary: In 2023, scientists relocated 246 endangered black abalone to a protected coastal site in California to help restore a population devastated by disease.
articles.body: In 2023, scientists relocated 246 endangered black abalone to a protected coastal site in California to help restore a population devastated by disease. Three years later, surveys recorded 302 individuals, compared with 54 before the intervention, while the density in high-quality habitat reached one abalone per square metre. Researchers also discovered juvenile abalone, raising hopes of renewed reproduction. According to a study published in Frontiers in Conservation Science, the results suggest that carefully planned relocation and habitat restoration could help the species recover. However, scientists say further monitoring is needed to establish whether the population can reproduce successfully and sustain itself over time.Why black abalone needed interventionBlack abalone (Haliotis cracherodii) is a marine mollusc found along the Pacific coast of North America, including California and Mexico. It lives on rocky shorelines in the intertidal zone, where it attaches itself to hard surfaces and feeds on algae. The species suffered severe population declines during the 1980s and 1990s because of withering syndrome, a disease associated with the bacterium Candidatus Xenohaliotis californiensis. Populations declined dramatically, and black abalone was listed as endangered under the US Endangered Species Act in 2009.Recovery has been difficult because black abalone reproduce by releasing eggs and sperm into the water. This method, known as broadcast spawning, works best when individuals live close enough together for fertilisation to occur. When populations become too sparse, reproduction becomes less successful, making natural recovery harder even when suitable habitat remains.How the relocation was carried outThe conservation project moved abalone from a recovering population on Santa Cruz Island to the Jack and Laura Dangermond Preserve in California. Although the receiving site offered suitable rocky habitat, its black abalone population had remained depleted following earlier disease-related losses.The relocation took place in two phases in 2023, with the first group moved in March and the second in October. Researchers also restored selected sections of rocky habitat by clearing some mussels, algae and other organisms that occupied spaces used by abalone.The project brought together scientists from the University of California, Santa Cruz, The Nature Conservancy and partner organisations. Researchers monitored the animals and surveyed the wider site to assess population numbers, habitat conditions and evidence of recruitment, the process through which young animals join a population. The researchers reported a mortality rate of 1.6% between collection and release, suggesting that the animals could be transported with relatively little immediate loss.Abalone numbers increased over three yearsThe results were encouraging. In March 2022, before the relocation, researchers counted 54 black abalone across 11,719 square metres of surveyed habitat. The number increased to 252 by March 2024 and reached 302 in February 2026. Density in high-quality habitat also rose, from 0.2 individuals per square metre in 2022 to 0.76 in 2024 and one per square metre in 2026. Greater density is important because black abalone need to live relatively close together for successful reproduction.Researchers estimated that more than 80% of the relocated animals were accounted for in surveys three years later, although tag loss and the difficulty of detecting animals in crevices prevented precise estimates of survival. Scientists therefore could not reliably distinguish every relocated abalone from those already living at the site. The increase in the overall count is promising, but it does not independently prove that the population has become self-sustaining.Juveniles offer hope for recoveryDuring the February 2026 survey, researchers recorded 12 juvenile black abalone measuring between 18 and 40 millimetres, along with six small adults measuring around 50 millimetres. The discovery was significant because juveniles had not been recorded at the site during monitoring and broader habitat surveys since the disease-related decline in 1993. Their presence suggests that conditions may once again support recruitment and the survival of young abalone.However, researchers have not yet established whether the juveniles were offspring of the relocated animals. Genetic parentage analysis will be needed to determine their origin. The findings therefore indicate possible renewed reproduction rather than definitive proof that the relocated population is breeding successfully.What happens next?The study shows how relocation, habitat restoration and long-term monitoring can help rebuild a depleted marine population. Researchers hope the approach will inform future black abalone restoration efforts, particularly along mainland southern California, where populations remain low.The next challenge is to establish whether young abalone survive to adulthood and whether the population can maintain itself without continued intervention. For now, the rise from 54 recorded individuals to 302, alongside the appearance of juveniles, offers encouraging evidence that carefully managed conservation can give this endangered species a better chance of recovery.

articles.title: In 2023, restoration began on 150 acres of California floodplain with more than 30,000 native plants; three years later, Swainson’s hawks have nested in Shasta County for the first confirmed time in about 30 years
articles.summary: A piece of abandoned farmland in California, once covered with weeds and unwanted grasses, has become home to a rare bird that had not been confirmed
articles.body: A piece of abandoned farmland in California, once covered with weeds and unwanted grasses, has become home to a rare bird that had not been confirmed nesting in the area for about 30 years. In 2023, conservation workers began restoring 150 acres of land near the Sacramento River. They planted more than 32,000 native trees and plants, and three years later, Swainson’s hawks have been found raising their young there.The discovery was made in Shasta County, where wildlife biologist Tobias Felbeck spotted the birds in a tall sycamore tree. Looking through his binoculars, he found a female hawk in a nest, along with an adult male and two young birds. It was the first confirmed nesting of Swainson’s hawks in the county in roughly three decades, according to conservation organisation River Partners.Swainson’s hawks are listed as threatened under California’s Endangered Species Act. They are more commonly found further south, particularly between Sacramento and Stockton.The finding is encouraging, although scientists say one nesting pair is not enough to confirm that the species is making a wider comeback. What makes the discovery interesting is that other rare birds have also started breeding in the same restored area. The changes offer an early indication of what can happen when damaged land is given the conditions needed to support wildlife again.What happened to the land before the birds returned?The restoration site, known as Rancho Breisgau, covers 306 acres near the point where Battle Creek joins the Sacramento River. Much of this land was previously used for farming, particularly walnut orchards. Over time, parts of the property were abandoned, allowing invasive weeds and grasses to spread.The problem was not simply that the land looked neglected. The unwanted plants had made it difficult for native trees and other vegetation to grow naturally. This also meant fewer suitable places for animals to find food, shelter and move between habitats.The location matters because it connects larger stretches of natural land along Battle Creek and the Sacramento River. When one section loses its native vegetation, animals that depend on these connected areas can struggle to move through them.To address this, River Partners began working with the US Bureau of Land Management (BLM) in autumn 2023. The first phase covered 150 acres. In October 2024, a large planting effort was organised with support from the Shasta Chapter of the California Native Plant Society.More than 32,000 native trees and plants were eventually introduced. The aim was to replace the damaged farmland with vegetation that naturally belongs in the area and provide better conditions for wildlife.The project is also intended to benefit fish. Battle Creek is one of California's remaining streams that support all four runs of Chinook salmon, as well as steelhead. Restoring land beside the river is part of the effort to improve their habitat.How did the hawks find their way back?As the newly planted vegetation began growing, insects returned to the area. These included grasshoppers and dragonflies, which Felbeck believes may have helped attract the Swainson’s hawks.The birds could have discovered the location while searching for a suitable nesting site. Although researchers cannot say exactly why they chose it, the presence of food and suitable nesting conditions offers a possible explanation.River Partners Director of Restoration Michael Rogner said the discovery could indicate that the hawks are beginning to move back into parts of their former range.“Seeing a little bit of range expansion into Shasta County could be some evidence that they are recolonizing more of their historic range,” he said.The hawks were not the only surprise. Later that summer, Felbeck heard an indigo bunting, a bird usually found in eastern parts of the United States. When conservationists investigated, they discovered that two indigo buntings were breeding at Rancho Breisgau.The pair was around 500 miles outside the species' established range. It was also the first confirmed breeding pair in Shasta County, where indigo buntings had previously been recorded only four times.Rare birds returning elsewhere in CaliforniaRancho Breisgau is not the only restored location where unusual wildlife sightings have been reported. In July 2026, endangered least Bell’s vireos were spotted at two sites in San Diego County. Two appeared at Otay Delta on July 21, while another was recorded at San Dieguito River Park two days later.Both locations had undergone restoration years earlier. River Partners planted 19,000 native trees and plants across 55 acres at Otay Delta in 2014. At San Dieguito River Park, 20,000 were planted across 100 acres in 2018.Least Bell’s vireos were once found across much of California's Central Valley, but their numbers declined as natural riverside vegetation disappeared. Their survival was also affected by brown-headed cowbirds, which lay eggs in other birds' nests, leaving those birds to raise their young.The vireos have gradually been expanding their breeding range northwards. Conservationists hope that restoring more connected stretches of natural habitat could eventually help them return to areas where they were previously common.Other animals have benefited from similar efforts. Endangered riparian woodrats were found in a restored forest in the San Joaquin River National Wildlife Refuge in 2024, while riparian brush rabbits have also been reported doing well in restored habitat nearby.
